* **Signals:** Use the `post_save` signal for automatic generation upon user creation.

REST framework uses permission classes to grant or deny API access. Permissions are defined as a list and checked before the view's main body runs; failure triggers an `exceptions.PermissionDenied` or `exceptions.NotAuthenticated` exception, resulting in either a 403 Forbidden or 401 Unauthorized response.

Key permission classes include:
* `AllowAny`: Unrestricted access.
* `IsAuthenticated`: Only registered users.
* `IsAdminUser`: Only users where `user.is_staff` is True.
* `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`: Full access for authenticated users; read-only access (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`) for unauthenticated users.

Additionally, object-level permissions determine if a user can act on a specific model instance and are triggered during `.get_object()` calls. Permissions can be composed using logical operators: `&` (and), `|` (or), and `~` (not), with brackets for grouping.

The requirements specify that only authenticated users can create snippets, and only the original creator can update or delete them, while unauthenticated users maintain full read-only access.

To achieve this, the `Snippet` model is updated with new fields to track the creator and store highlighted HTML. In the serializers, a `ReadOnlyField` (or `CharField(read_only=True)`) is used for serialized representations that should not be used during deserialization. The simplest style of permission would be to allow access to any authenticated user, and deny access to any unauthenticated user. This corresponds to the

A slightly less strict style of permission would be to allow full access to authenticated users, but allow read-only access to unauthenticated users. This corresponds to the

or
`exceptions.NotAuthenticated`
exception will be raised, and the main body of the view will not run.

When the permission checks fail, either a "403 Forbidden" or a "401 Unauthorized" response will be returned, according to the following rules:

Global permissions are checked against all requests, while object-level permissions apply to specific object instances. To enforce object-level permissions in custom views or overridden `get_object` methods, you must explicitly call `.check_object_permissions(request, obj)`, which raises `PermissionDenied` or `NotAuthenticated` upon failure. To distinguish between read and write operations, use the `SAFE_METHODS` constant (`GET`, `OPTIONS`, `HEAD`). Custom permission classes can also define `message` and `code` attributes to customize exception details. For the browsable API, login and logout views are added by including `rest_framework.urls` in the project's `urls.py`.

To restrict editing and deleting snippets to only their creators, a custom `IsOwnerOrReadOnly` permission class is created in `permissions.py` and added to the `SnippetDetail` view. 

Regarding authentication, the API defaults to `SessionAuthentication` and `BasicAuthentication`. While browser interactions use session-based login, programmatic requests must explicitly provide credentials (such as username and password) to avoid authentication errors when attempting to create or modify snippets.

## API Reference¶ {#api-reference}

### AllowAny¶ {#allowany}

The
`AllowAny`
permission class will allow unrestricted access,
regardless of if the request was authenticated or unauthenticated
.

This permission is not strictly required, since you can achieve the same result by using an empty list or tuple for the permissions setting, but you may find it useful to specify this class because it makes the intention explicit.

### IsAuthenticated¶ {#isauthenticated}

The
`IsAuthenticated`
permission class will deny permission to any unauthenticated user, and allow permission otherwise.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to registered users.

Permissions are used to grant or deny access for different classes of users to different parts of the API.

The simplest style of permission would be to allow access to any authenticated user, and deny access to any unauthenticated user. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticated`
class in REST framework.

A slightly less strict style of permission would be to allow full access to authenticated users, but allow read-only access to unauthenticated users. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
class in REST framework.

## How permissions are determined¶ {#how-permissions-are-determined}

Permissions in REST framework are always defined as a list of permission classes.

Before running the main body of the view each permission in the list is checked.
If any permission check fails, an
`exceptions.PermissionDenied`
or
`exceptions.NotAuthenticated`
exception will be raised, and the main body of the view will not run.

When the permission checks fail, either a "403 Forbidden" or a "401 Unauthorized" response will be returned, according to the following rules:

The request was successfully authenticated, but permission was denied.
— An HTTP 403 Forbidden response will be returned.

## Unauthorized and Forbidden responses¶ {#unauthorized-and-forbidden-responses}

When an unauthenticated request is denied permission there are two different error codes that may be appropriate.

HTTP 401 Unauthorized (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.2)
HTTP 403 Permission Denied (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.4)

HTTP 401 responses must always include a
`WWW-Authenticate`
header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.  HTTP 403 responses do not include the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header.

The kind of response that will be used depends on the authentication scheme.  Although multiple authentication schemes may be in use, only one scheme may be used to determine the type of response.
The first authentication class set on the view is used when determining the type of response
.

Note that when a request may successfully authenticate, but still be denied permission to perform the request, in which case a
`403 Permission Denied`
response will always be used, regardless of the authentication scheme.

REST framework uses permission classes to grant or deny API access. Permissions are defined as a list and checked before the view's main body runs; failure triggers an `exceptions.PermissionDenied` or `exceptions.NotAuthenticated` exception, resulting in either a 403 Forbidden or 401 Unauthorized response.

Key permission classes include:
* `AllowAny`: Unrestricted access.
* `IsAuthenticated`: Only registered users.
* `IsAdminUser`: Only users where `user.is_staff` is True.
* `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`: Full access for authenticated users; read-only access (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`) for unauthenticated users.

Additionally, object-level permissions determine if a user can act on a specific model instance and are triggered during `.get_object()` calls. Permissions can be composed using logical operators: `&` (and), `|` (or), and `~` (not), with brackets for grouping.

## Object level permissions¶ {#object-level-permissions}

REST framework permissions also support object-level permissioning.  Object level permissions are used to determine if a user should be allowed to act on a particular object, which will typically be a model instance.

Object level permissions are run by REST framework's generic views when
`.get_object()`
is called.
As with view level permissions, an
`exceptions.PermissionDenied`
exception will be raised if the user is not allowed to act on the given object.

The goal is to implement authentication and permissions for an API to ensure code snippets are associated with a creator. The requirements specify that only authenticated users can create snippets, and only the original creator can update or delete them, while unauthenticated users maintain full read-only access.

To achieve this, the `Snippet` model is updated with new fields to track the creator and store highlighted HTML. In the serializers, a `ReadOnlyField` (or `CharField(read_only=True)`) is used for serialized representations that should not be used during deserialization. To enforce access control in the views, the `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly` permission class is utilized, granting read-write access to authenticated users and read-only access to unauthenticated requests.

### LimitOffsetPagination¶ {#limitoffsetpagination}

This pagination style mirrors the syntax used when looking up multiple database records. The client includes both a "limit" and an
"offset" query parameter. The limit indicates the maximum number of items to return, and is equivalent to the

Request

`GET https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=400`


Response
:


`HTTP200OK{"count":1023,"next":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=500","previous":"https://api.example.org/accounts/?limit=100&offset=300","results":[…]}`

`LimitOffsetPagination`

Setting `pagination_class` to `None` disables pagination.

Key pagination styles include:
* **PageNumberPagination**: The default style.
* **LimitOffsetPagination**: Uses "limit" (maximum items) and "offset" (starting position) query parameters. It can be customized by overriding attributes like `default_limit`, `limit_query_param`, and `offset_query_param`.
* **CursorPagination**: Uses an opaque cursor for forward and reverse navigation, requiring a unique, unchanging ordering of items.

Additionally, generic views utilize `filter_backends` for queryset filtering and the `get_queryset()` method to determine the base queryset for list and detail views.

# Pagination¶ {#pagination}

Django provides a few classes that help you manage paginated data – that is, data that’s split across several pages, with “Previous/Next” links.
—
Django documentation (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/pagination/)

REST framework includes support for customizable pagination styles. This allows you to modify how large result sets are split into individual pages of data.

The pagination API can support either:

Pagination links that are provided as part of the content of the response.
Pagination links that are included in response headers, such as
`Content-Range`
or
`Link`
.

The built-in styles currently all use links included as part of the content of the response. This style is more accessible when using the browsable API.

Pagination is only performed automatically if you're using the generic views or viewsets. If you're using a regular
`APIView`
, you'll need to call into the pagination API yourself to ensure you return a paginated response.

Django REST framework provides customizable pagination to split large result sets into pages. Pagination is automatic for generic views and viewsets, but must be manually called in regular `APIView` classes. Links can be included in the response content or headers (e.g., `Link` or `Content-Range`).

The `PageNumberPagination` class allows overrides for `page_size`, `page_query_param`, `page_size_query_param`, and `django_paginator_class`. Developers can create custom pagination by overriding `get_paginated_response` or using the low-level API (`display_page_controls`, `.to_html()`, and `.get_html_context()`).

Third-party packages extend these capabilities:
* **DRF-extensions**: Adds `PaginateByMaxMixin` for `?page_size=max` requests.
* **drf-proxy-pagination**: Provides `ProxyPagination` to select pagination classes via query parameters.
* **link-header-pagination**: Offers `LinkHeaderPagination` for HTTP `Link` header pagination.

## Custom generic filtering¶ {#custom-generic-filtering}

You can also provide your own generic filtering backend, or write an installable app for other developers to use.

To do so override
`BaseFilterBackend`
, and override the
`.filter_queryset(self, request, queryset, view)`
method.  The method should return a new, filtered queryset.

As well as allowing clients to perform searches and filtering, generic filter backends can be useful for restricting which objects should be visible to any given request or user.

### Example¶ {#example}

For example, you might need to restrict users to only being able to see objects they created.


`classIsOwnerFilterBackend(filters.BaseFilterBackend):"""
Filter that only allows users to see their own objects.
"""deffilter_queryset(self,request,queryset,view):returnqueryset.filter(owner=request.user)`

## Generic Filtering¶ {#generic-filtering}

As well as being able to override the default queryset, REST framework also includes support for generic filtering backends that allow you to easily construct complex searches and filters.

Generic filters can also present themselves as HTML controls in the browsable API and admin API.

### Setting filter backends¶ {#setting-filter-backends}

`DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS`
setting. For example.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS':['django_filters.rest_framework.DjangoFilterBackend']}`


You can also set the filter backends on a per-view, or per-viewset basis,
using the
`GenericAPIView`
class-based views.

*   **SerializerMethodField**: A read-only field that retrieves its value by calling a method on the serializer class. By default, it looks for a method named `get_<field_name>`, which accepts the object being serialized and returns the desired data for the serialized representation.

Django REST framework handles validation through serializer classes using field-level validators, object-level `.validate()` methods, and reusable validators in the `Meta` class. Specific validator classes like `UniqueValidator`, `UniqueTogetherValidator`, and `UniqueForDate/Month/YearValidator` enforce uniqueness constraints. Custom validation can also be implemented via `.validate_<field_name>` methods or by overriding `to_internal_value`.

`ModelSerializer` automatically generates fields and validators, though explicit `Serializer` classes are recommended for complex cases. Special field types like `HiddenField` and `CreateOnlyDefault` manage data that should not be client-editable. For nested representations, serializers can be assigned to fields, with `many=True` for lists.

REST framework provides several validator classes to enforce uniqueness constraints on serializer fields and classes:

*   **UniqueValidator**: Enforces `unique=True` on serializer fields using a required `queryset`, an optional `message`, and a `lookup` (defaults to 'exact').
*   **UniqueTogetherValidator**: Enforces `unique_together` constraints on serializer classes. It requires a `queryset` and a list of `fields`. It implicitly treats these fields as required unless they have default values.
*   **UniqueForDate/Month/YearValidator**: Enforce date-range uniqueness on serializer classes, requiring a `queryset`, a `field`, and a `date_field`.

During updates, uniqueness validators exclude the current instance. However, this exclusion is not possible for nested serializers, requiring manual validation in the view or `.validate()` method. To debug automatically generated validators in `ModelSerializer`, users can inspect a serializer instance via `manage.py shell`.

### Updating nested serializers¶ {#updating-nested-serializers}

When applying an update to an existing instance, uniqueness validators will
exclude the current instance from the uniqueness check. The current instance
is available in the context of the uniqueness check, because it exists as
an attribute on the serializer, having initially been passed using
`instance=...`
when instantiating the serializer.

In the case of update operations on
nested
serializers there's no way of
applying this exclusion, because the instance is not available.

Again, you'll probably want to explicitly remove the validator from the
serializer class, and write the code for the validation constraint
explicitly, in a
`.validate()`
method, or in the view.

### Debugging complex cases¶ {#debugging-complex-cases}

If you're not sure exactly what behavior a
`ModelSerializer`
class will
generate it is usually a good idea to run
`manage.py shell`
, and print
an instance of the serializer, so that you can inspect the fields and
validators that it automatically generates for you.

Note
The
`UniqueTogetherValidator`
class always imposes an implicit constraint that all the fields it applies to are always treated as required. Fields with
`default`
values are an exception to this as they always supply a value even when omitted from user input.

The provided text describes three specific serializer field classes:

*   **HiddenField**: A field that takes values from a default or callable rather than user input. It is primarily used for validation without exposing fields to the end user and does not appear in `partial=True` serializers during `PATCH` requests.
*   **ModelField**: A generic field tied to an arbitrary model field that delegates serialization and deserialization to that associated field. It is used by `ModelSerializer` for custom model field classes and is generally intended for internal use.
*   **SerializerMethodField**: A read-only field that retrieves its value by calling a method on the serializer class. By default, it looks for a method named `get_<field_name>`, which accepts the object being serialized and returns the desired data for the serialized representation.

To opt-out from default fields, see

user_input: What does write_only=True on a field do?
reference: It makes the field usable for create/update but keeps it out of serialized output — handy for passwords.
reference_contexts: Set this to True to ensure that the field may be used when updating or creating an instance, but is not included when serializing the representation.

llm_references:
Serializer field constructors accept several core arguments:

*   **read_only**: If `True`, the field is included in output but ignored during create/update operations.
*   **write_only**: If `True`, the field is used for create/update but excluded from output.
*   **required**: Defaults to `True`. If `False`, the field is not mandatory during deserialization and may be omitted from output.
*   **default**: Provides a value if none is supplied. It can be a callable and implies the field is not required; using both `default` and `required` raises an error.
*   **allow_null**: If `True`, `None` is a valid value.
*   **source**: Specifies the attribute used to populate the field. It supports methods, dotted notation for traversal, or `'*'` to pass the entire object. Dotted notation may require a `default` and can cause n+1 database problems if not handled with `select_related` or `prefetch_related`.

### Altered the behavior ofread_onlyplusdefaulton Field.¶ {#altered-the-behavior-of-read_only-plus-default-on-field}

#5886 (https://github.com/encode/django-rest-framework/issues/5886)
`read_only`
fields will now
always
be excluded from writable fields.

Previously
`read_only`
fields when combined with a
`default`

`default`
for create and update
operations. This was counter-intuitive in some circumstances and led to difficulties supporting dotted
`source`
attributes on nullable relations.

In order to maintain the old behavior you may need to pass the value of
`read_only`
fields when calling
`save()`
in
the view:


`defperform_create(self,serializer):serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)`


Alternatively you may override
`save()`
or
`create()`
or
`update()`
on the serializer as appropriate.

## Core arguments¶ {#core-arguments}

Each serializer field class constructor takes at least these arguments.  Some Field classes take additional, field-specific arguments, but the following should always be accepted:

### read_only¶ {#read_only}

Read-only fields are included in the API output, but should not be included in the input during create or update operations. Any 'read_only' fields that are incorrectly included in the serializer input will be ignored.

Set this to
`True`
to ensure that the field is used when serializing a representation, but is not used when creating or updating an instance during deserialization.

Defaults to
`False`

### write_only¶ {#write_only}

Set this to
`True`
to ensure that the field may be used when updating or creating an instance, but is not included when serializing the representation.

Defaults to
`False`

### required¶ {#required}

Normally an error will be raised if a field is not supplied during deserialization.
Set to false if this field is not required to be present during deserialization.

Setting this to
`False`
also allows the object attribute or dictionary key to be omitted from output when serializing the instance.

## Advanced field defaults¶ {#advanced-field-defaults}

Validators that are applied across multiple fields in the serializer can sometimes require a field input that should not be provided by the API client, but that
is
available as input to the validator.
For this purposes use
`HiddenField`
. This field will be present in
`validated_data`
but
will not
be used in the serializer output representation.

Note
Using a
`read_only=True`
field is excluded from writable fields so it won't use a
`default=…`
argument. Look
3.8 announcement (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/community/3.8-announcement/#altered-the-behavior-of-read_only-plus-default-on-field)
.

REST framework includes a couple of defaults that may be useful in this context.

### CurrentUserDefault¶ {#currentuserdefault}

A default class that can be used to represent the current user. In order to use this, the 'request' must have been provided as part of the context dictionary when instantiating the serializer.

`min_length`
- Validates that the input contains no fewer than this number of characters.
`allow_blank`
- If set to
`True`
then the empty string should be considered a valid value. If set to
`False`
then the empty string is considered invalid and will raise a validation error. Defaults to
`False`
.
`trim_whitespace`
- If set to
`True`
then leading and trailing whitespace is trimmed. Defaults to
`True`
.

The
`allow_null`
option is also available for string fields, although its usage is discouraged in favor of
`allow_blank`
. It is valid to set both
`allow_blank=True`
and
`allow_null=True`
, but doing so means that there will be two differing types of empty value permissible for string representations, which can lead to data inconsistencies and subtle application bugs.

### EmailField¶ {#emailfield}

A text representation, validates the text to be a valid email address.

If set to
`False`
then filename string values will be used for the output representation. Defaults to the value of the
`UPLOADED_FILES_USE_URL`
settings key, which is
`True`
unless set otherwise.

Requires either the
`Pillow`
package or
`PIL`
package.  The
`Pillow`
package is recommended, as
`PIL`
is no longer actively maintained.

## Core arguments¶ {#core-arguments}

Each serializer field class constructor takes at least these arguments.  Some Field classes take additional, field-specific arguments, but the following should always be accepted:

### read_only¶ {#read_only}

Read-only fields are included in the API output, but should not be included in the input during create or update operations. Any 'read_only' fields that are incorrectly included in the serializer input will be ignored.

Set this to
`True`
to ensure that the field is used when serializing a representation, but is not used when creating or updating an instance during deserialization.

Defaults to
`False`

### write_only¶ {#write_only}

Set this to
`True`
to ensure that the field may be used when updating or creating an instance, but is not included when serializing the representation.

Defaults to
`False`

### required¶ {#required}

Normally an error will be raised if a field is not supplied during deserialization.
Set to false if this field is not required to be present during deserialization.

Setting this to
`False`
also allows the object attribute or dictionary key to be omitted from output when serializing the instance.

To opt-out from default fields, see
Specifying which fields to include (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/serializers/#specifying-which-fields-to-include)
.

The provided text describes several relation fields used in serializers to represent relationships:

*   **StringRelatedField**: A read-only field that represents the target using its string representation.
*   **PrimaryKeyRelatedField**: Represents the target using its primary key. It is read-write by default and requires either a `queryset` for lookups or `read_only=True`.
*   **HyperlinkedRelatedField**: Represents the target via a hyperlink. It is read-write by default and is designed for objects mapping to a URL with a single keyword argument.
*   **SlugRelatedField**: Represents the target using a unique slug field. It is read-write by default and requires a `queryset` or `read_only=True`.

Common arguments across these fields include `many` (set to `True` for to-many relationships) and `allow_null` (allows `None` or empty strings). `PrimaryKeyRelatedField` also supports `pk_field` to control primary key serialization.

### Customizing the HTML display¶ {#customizing-the-html-display}

The built-in
`__str__`
method of the model will be used to generate string representations of the objects used to populate the
`choices`

To provide customized representations for such inputs, override
`display_value()`
of a
`RelatedField`
subclass. This method will receive a model object, and should return a string suitable for representing it. For example:


`classTrackPrimaryKeyRelatedField(serializers.PrimaryKeyRelatedField):defdisplay_value(self,instance):return'Track: %s'%(instance.title)`


### Select field cutoffs¶ {#select-field-cutoffs}

When rendered in the browsable API relational fields will default to only displaying a maximum of 1000 selectable items. If more items are present then a disabled option with "More than 1000 items…" will be displayed.

This behavior is intended to prevent a template from being unable to render in an acceptable timespan due to a very large number of relationships being displayed.

## Custom relational fields¶ {#custom-relational-fields}

In rare cases where none of the existing relational styles fit the representation you need,
you can implement a completely custom relational field, that describes exactly how the
output representation should be generated from the model instance.

To implement a custom relational field, you should override
`RelatedField`
, and implement the
`.to_representation(self, value)`
method. This method takes the target of the field as the
`value`
argument, and should return the representation that should be used to serialize the target. The
`value`
argument will typically be a model instance.

If you want to implement a read-write relational field, you must also implement the
.to_internal_value(self, data) method (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/serializers/#to_internal_valueself-data)
.

To provide a dynamic queryset based on the
`context`
, you can also override
`.get_queryset(self)`
instead of specifying
`.queryset`
on the class or when initializing the field.

Relational fields in Django REST framework represent model relationships, including `ForeignKey`, `ManyToManyField`, `OneToOneField`, reverse relationships, and `GenericForeignKey`. While declared in `relations.py`, they should be imported from the `serializers` module.

For writable relationship fields, an explicit `queryset` argument is required for model instance lookups. Relational fields targeting a `ManyToManyField` with a `through` model are read-only by default; extra fields on such models can be serialized as nested objects.

Custom relational fields can be created by overriding `RelatedField` and implementing `.to_representation()`, and `.to_internal_value()` for read-write functionality. Additionally, `.get_queryset()` can be overridden for dynamic querysets.

REST Framework does not automatically optimize querysets with `select_related` or `prefetch_related`. Third-party packages like `drf-nested-routers`, `rest-framework-generic-relations`, and `rest-framework-gm2m-relations` offer extended functionality for nested resources and generic foreign keys.

The provided text explains how to handle different types of relationships in serializers. For generic foreign keys, a custom field must be defined to explicitly determine how targets are serialized. This is achieved by overriding the `.to_representation()` method, which can return a simple textual representation or a nested representation using specific serializers based on the instance type. Conversely, reverse generic keys using `GenericRelation` can be serialized with regular relational field types because the target type is known. Additionally, the text notes that relational fields targeting a `ManyToManyField` with a specified `through` model are read-only by default.

# Parsers¶ {#parsers}

Machine interacting web services tend to use more
structured formats for sending data than form-encoded, since they're
sending more complex data than simple forms
— Malcom Tredinnick,
Django developers group (https://groups.google.com/d/topic/django-developers/dxI4qVzrBY4/discussion)

REST framework includes a number of built-in Parser classes, that allow you to accept requests with various media types.  There is also support for defining your own custom parsers, which gives you the flexibility to design the media types that your API accepts.

## How the parser is determined¶ {#how-the-parser-is-determined}

The set of valid parsers for a view is always defined as a list of classes.  When
`request.data`
is accessed, REST framework will examine the
`Content-Type`
header on the incoming request, and determine which parser to use to parse the request content.

The REST framework uses parsers and renderers to handle API data input and output via content negotiation, which examines the `Accept` header or URL suffixes. Parsers, such as `JSONParser`, `FormParser`, `MultiPartParser`, and `FileUploadParser`, populate `request.data`. Renderers, including `JSONRenderer`, `TemplateHTMLRenderer`, `StaticHTMLRenderer`, and `BrowsableAPIRenderer`, format responses into byte streams.

Renderers can be configured globally via `DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES` or per view using `renderer_classes` or the `@api_view` decorator. Custom renderers and parsers can be created by overriding `BaseRenderer` and `BaseParser`. Additionally, third-party packages extend support for formats like YAML, XML, CSV, Excel, and Msgpack. The framework also handles content negotiation errors with a `415 Unsupported Media Type` response and supports flexible authentication policies.

Django REST framework simplifies API routing by emphasizing absolute URIs via `reverse` and `reverse_lazy`. It provides `SimpleRouter` and `DefaultRouter` to automate URL configuration for viewsets, with `DefaultRouter` adding an API root and `.json` suffix support. Routers use a `register()` method requiring a `prefix` and `viewset`, with an optional `basename` necessary if no `.queryset` attribute exists.

Customization is achieved through the `@action` decorator for additional methods, subclassing routers, or overriding `BaseRouter`. For advanced needs, `drf-nested-routers` and `DRF-extensions` support nested resources, while `wq.db` offers a `ModelRouter` for model-based registration. Developers can manage instance matching via `lookup_field` and customize URL patterns using `include` for namespacing. Additionally, setting `use_regex_path` to `False` enables path converters, and the `trailing_slash` argument can be disabled to remove conventional trailing slashes.

Generally we recommend a flat style for API representations where possible, but the nested URL style can also be reasonable when used in moderation.

## Further notes¶ {#further-notes}

### Thequerysetargument¶ {#the-queryset-argument}

The
`queryset`
argument is only ever required for
writable
relationship field, in which case it is used for performing the model instance lookup, that maps from the primitive user input, into a model instance.

In version 2.x a serializer class could
sometimes
automatically determine the
`queryset`
argument
if
a
`ModelSerializer`
class was being used.

This behavior is now replaced with
always
using an explicit
`queryset`
argument for writable relational fields.

Doing so reduces the amount of hidden 'magic' that
`ModelSerializer`
provides, makes the behavior of the field more clear, and ensures that it is trivial to move between using the
`ModelSerializer`
shortcut, or using fully explicit
`Serializer`
classes.

Django REST framework manages API access through authentication, throttling, and permission classes, which can be set globally or per-view. Routing is simplified using `SimpleRouter` and `DefaultRouter` to automate URL configurations for viewsets. Model relationships are handled via relational fields, with nested relationships implemented through serializers.

Data input and output are managed by parsers (e.g., `JSONParser`) and renderers (e.g., `JSONRenderer`) via content negotiation. The `Request` class extends Django's `HttpRequest`, providing `request.data` for parsed body content and `request.query_params` for query strings. Additionally, the framework supports OpenAPI 3 schema generation through `SchemaGenerator` and `AutoSchema`, though `drf-spectacular` is the preferred modern alternative. Performance optimization for relationships requires the use of `select_related` or `prefetch_related`. Customization is possible across all these components by subclassing base classes or using decorators.

Further 3.x releases will present simple upgrades, without the same level of fundamental API changes necessary for the 3.0 release.

The central feature that distinguishes the REST architectural style from other network-based styles is its emphasis on a uniform interface between components.
— Roy Fielding,
Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures (https://www.ics.uci.edu/~fielding/pubs/dissertation/rest_arch_style.htm#sec_5_1_5)

As a rule, it's probably better practice to return absolute URIs from your Web APIs, such as
`http://example.com/foobar`
, rather than returning relative URIs, such as
`/foobar`
.

The advantages of doing so are:

It's more explicit.
It leaves less work for your API clients.

It makes it easy to do things like markup HTML representations with hyperlinks.

The DRF-native approach for token-based authentication is to use `TokenAuthentication`. This method allows clients to authenticate by including a token key in the `Authorization` HTTP header, prefixed by "Token".

To implement this, follow these steps:

1.  **Installation and Configuration:** Add `rest_framework.authtoken` to your `INSTALLED_APPS` setting.
2.  **Database Setup:** Run `manage.py migrate` to create the necessary tables for storing tokens.
3.  **Endpoint Implementation:** Add the `obtain_auth_token` view to your URLconf. This provides the endpoint where users can exchange their username and password for a token.
4.  **Production Requirement:** Ensure your API uses `https` for security.

Once configured, tokens can be generated automatically via signals upon user creation, manually through the Django Admin interface, or via a management command (`./manage.py drf_create_token <username>`).

## Django 5.1+LoginRequiredMiddleware¶ {#django-51-loginrequiredmiddleware}

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)

To achieve this, you should implement a custom permission class that checks if the user requesting the action is the owner of the object. 

In your view, you can apply this custom permission to ensure that while read-only access is granted to everyone, write and delete operations are restricted to the creator. 

The structure involves the following steps:

1.  **Create a custom permission class**: Define a class that inherits from `BasePermission`. Within this class, implement the `has_object_permission` method. This method should return `True` for safe methods (like `GET`, `HEAD`, or `OPTIONS`) to allow read access to everyone. For other methods, it should check if `request.user` matches the object's owner (e.g., `obj.owner == request.user`).
2.  **Apply the permission to your views**: Assign this custom permission class to the `permission_classes` attribute of your view.
3.  **Associate records with users**: Ensure your model has a field (such as `owner`) that tracks the creator. When creating a record, override the `perform_create` method in your view to save the `request.user` as the owner of the instance.
4.  **Use `ReadOnlyField` in serializers**: Use a `ReadOnlyField` for the owner field in your serializer to ensure the creator is automatically associated with the record and cannot be modified by the user during updates.

By combining a custom permission class that checks object ownership with the standard `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly` logic, you ensure that unauthenticated users can browse the data, while only the original creator has the authority to modify or delete their specific records.

reference: Don't take it from request data. In a generic view override perform_create to save with user=self.request.user, or on the serializer use a HiddenField with default=CurrentUserDefault so the current user is injected at save.

llm_response:
To automatically set the owner of a record to the currently logged-in user without requiring the client to send it, you can use the `CurrentUserDefault` class in your serializer. 

Define the field in your serializer as follows:

```python
owner = serializers.HiddenField(default=serializers.CurrentUserDefault())
```

By using `HiddenField`, the field will not be included in the serialized output, and `CurrentUserDefault` will automatically populate the field with the user from the request during the creation process.

Alternatively, if you are using class-based views, you can override the `perform_create` method in your view to associate the user:

```python
def perform_create(self, serializer):
    serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)
```

In this approach, the `owner` field should be defined in your serializer as a `ReadOnlyField` to ensure it is included in the representation but not accepted as input during deserialization:

```python
owner = serializers.ReadOnlyField(source="owner.username")
```

To manage request rates for anonymous and logged-in users, you can use the built-in `AnonRateThrottle` and `UserRateThrottle` classes. These are defined as a list of classes within your project's settings.

The mechanism for setting the specific limits is the `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES` setting. You define the rates by mapping the throttle type to a string representing the frequency, using a `/` separator followed by the time period (e.g., 'day'). You only need to provide the first character of the time period (e.g., 'd' for day).

For example, you can configure your settings as follows:

REST_FRAMEWORK = {

        'rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle',
        'rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle',
    ],

}

Throttling in Django REST framework controls the rate of client requests to an API and is defined as a list of classes. It is intended for implementing business tiers and preventing service over-use, rather than as a security measure against DoS attacks or brute forcing. Multiple throttles can be used to handle different authentication levels, resource-intensive services, or both burst and sustained rates.

Built-in throttles use Django's cache framework and may be subject to race conditions under high concurrency. reference: Filter the queryset per request: override get_queryset to restrict results to request.user's objects, because object-level permissions aren't applied across a list for performance reasons.
reference_contexts: The simplest way to filter the queryset of any view that subclasses GenericAPIView is to override the .get_queryset() method.
You can do so by filtering based on the value of request.user .

llm_response:
To ensure users only see and edit their own objects, you should implement the following approach:

*   **Filter List Endpoints:** Override the `get_queryset()` method in your views to filter the results based on the current user. This ensures that list endpoints only return objects belonging to the authenticated user.
*   **Enforce Object-Level Permissions:** Create a custom permission class by overriding `BasePermission` and implementing the `has_object_permission()` method. This method should verify that the object's owner matches the `request.user`.
*   **Apply Permissions:** Use the custom permission class on your views to restrict access to specific object instances. If you are writing custom views, ensure you manually call `self.check_object_permissions(request, obj)` once you have the object instance to trigger these checks.
*   **Handle Object Creation:** When creating new objects, override the `perform_create()` method in your view to automatically associate the `request.user` as the owner of the new instance. 

If you are using `django-guardian` for object-level permissions, you can also utilize the `DjangoObjectPermissionsFilter` class to ensure that list endpoints automatically exclude objects for which the user lacks appropriate view permissions.

To implement authentication and permissions in a Django REST Framework API, the `Snippet` model is updated to track creators. Access is managed using `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`, allowing authenticated users read-write access while others remain read-only. A custom `IsOwnerOrReadOnly` permission class ensures only the original creator can update or delete specific snippets.

The API utilizes `SessionAuthentication` and `BasicAuthentication`, with `rest_framework.urls` added for browsable API login/logout. To associate snippets with users, the `SnippetList` view overrides `perform_create()` to save the `request.user` as the owner. Django REST framework uses permissions, alongside authentication and throttling, to determine if a request is granted or denied access. Permission checks run at the start of a view, typically utilizing `request.user` and `request.auth`.

Policies can be set globally via `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES` or on a per-view basis using `permission_classes`. To create custom permissions, override `BasePermission` and implement `has_permission()` and/or `has_object_permission()`.

Most provided permission classes do not implement object-level checks except for `DjangoObjectPermissions`. Object-level permissions are not automatically applied to list views for performance reasons or during object creation because `get_object()` is not called; the latter requires checks in the Serializer or `perform_create()` method. Access restrictions can be further customized using `get_queryset()` to limit visibility or `get_permissions()` for action-based checks.

Django REST framework offers several ways to implement API views. Class-based views provide a powerful pattern for reusing common functionality and keeping code DRY. ViewSets further abstract this by grouping common behaviors into classes, allowing developers to focus on API interactions and state rather than URL construction. Unlike standard View classes, ViewSets use operations like `retrieve` and `update` instead of method handlers like `get` or `put`.

ViewSets are typically bound to URLs using a Router class, such as `DefaultRouter`, which automatically generates the URL conf and the API root view. Custom endpoints can be added to ViewSets using the `@action` decorator. While ViewSets ensure consistent URL conventions and reduce code, they are less explicit than individual views. For greater control, developers can use regular class-based views and define the URL conf explicitly.

To ensure your hyperlinked serializers produce fully qualified, absolute URLs instead of relative ones, you must include the current `request` in the serializer context when instantiating the serializer.

You can do this by passing the request object as follows:

`serializer = AccountSerializer(queryset, context={'request': request})`

By including the `request` in the context, the serializer is able to determine the appropriate hostname to generate absolute URLs. If you were to explicitly pass `{'request': None}` in the context, the serializer would default to using relative URLs.

To version the behavior of a view in Django REST framework, you can utilize the `request.version` attribute, which contains the version string requested by the client. 

You can vary the API's behavior by checking this attribute within your view methods. A common approach is to override methods like `get_serializer_class` to return different serializers based on the requested version. For example:

```python
def get_serializer_class(self):
    if self.request.version == 'v1':
        return AccountSerializerVersion1
    return AccountSerializer
```

To ensure this works correctly, you must enable versioning by configuring the `DEFAULT_VERSIONING_CLASS` in your settings or by setting the `versioning_class` attribute on your view. Additionally, if you are using hyperlinked serializers or reversing URLs, you must pass the `request` object as context or a keyword argument to ensure that generated URLs correctly reflect the requested version.

Key settings include `ORDERING_PARAM` for result ordering and several versioning configurations: `DEFAULT_VERSION` (the fallback version), `ALLOWED_VERSIONS` (restricts valid versions), `VERSION_PARAM` (the string used for versioning parameters), and `DEFAULT_VERSIONING_CLASS`.

Versioning can be configured globally or on a per-view/viewset basis using class variables. Available schemes include `AcceptHeaderVersioning`, which uses the `Accept` header, and `QueryParameterVersioning`. To implement a custom versioning scheme, developers should subclass `BaseVersioning` and override the `.determine_version` method. If the scheme is URL-based, the `.reverse()` method should also be overridden.

## CORS¶ {#cors}

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (https://www.w3.org/TR/cors/)
is a mechanism for allowing clients to interact with APIs that are hosted on a different domain.

The provided text outlines authentication and error handling in the Django REST framework (DRF). Unauthenticated requests denied permission return either an HTTP 401 Unauthorized (which must include a `WWW-Authenticate` header) or an HTTP 403 Forbidden, depending on the authentication scheme. However, a 403 response is always used if a successfully authenticated request is denied permission.

Key technical details include:
- **Middleware:** DRF views are opted-out of Django 5.1+ `LoginRequiredMiddleware`; instead, use `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`.
- **Deployment:** Apache mod_wsgi requires the `WSGIPassAuthorization On` directive to pass authorization headers.
- **SessionAuthentication:** Requires CSRF tokens for unsafe HTTP methods (PUT, PATCH, POST, DELETE).
- **Exceptions:** `NotAuthenticated` typically results in a 401 or 403 status, `PermissionDenied` results in a 403, and `NotFound` results in a 404.

This means that only authenticated requests require CSRF tokens, and anonymous requests may be sent without CSRF tokens. This behavior is not suitable for login views, which should always have CSRF validation applied.

To prevent Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks, "safe" HTTP operations (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`) must not alter server-side state, and "unsafe" operations (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`) must require a valid CSRF token. Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) allows clients to interact with APIs on different domains via specific server response headers. The recommended approach in REST framework is to handle CORS through middleware, such as using the `django-cors-headers` package, to ensure transparent support without modifying view behavior.

## CORS¶ {#cors}

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (https://www.w3.org/TR/cors/)
is a mechanism for allowing clients to interact with APIs that are hosted on a different domain.  CORS works by requiring the server to include a specific set of headers that allow a browser to determine if and when cross-domain requests should be allowed.

The best way to deal with CORS in REST framework is to add the required response headers in middleware.  This ensures that CORS is supported transparently, without having to change any behavior in your views.

Adam Johnson (https://github.com/adamchainz)
maintains the
django-cors-headers (https://github.com/adamchainz/django-cors-headers)
package, which is known to work correctly with REST framework APIs.

Note that when a request may successfully authenticate, but still be denied permission to perform the request, in which case a
`403 Permission Denied`
response will always be used, regardless of the authentication scheme.

## Django 5.1+LoginRequiredMiddleware¶ {#django-51-loginrequiredmiddleware}

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)
, please note that all views from DRF are opted-out of this middleware.  This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

To accept a raw file upload from a native client, you should use the `FileUploadParser`. Because this parser matches any content type, it should generally be the only parser configured on your API view.

You can set up the parser in your view as follows:

class FileUploadView(views.APIView):

    def put(self, request, filename, format=None):
        file_obj = request.data['file']
        # ... handle the file ...

The

permission class will allow unrestricted access,

This permission is not strictly required, since you can achieve the same result by using an empty list or tuple for the permissions setting, but you may find it useful to specify this class because it makes the intention explicit.

The provided text explains how to implement and manage permissions in a REST framework. Global permissions are checked against all requests, while object-level permissions apply to specific object instances. To enforce object-level permissions in custom views or overridden `get_object` methods, you must explicitly call `.check_object_permissions(request, obj)`, which raises `PermissionDenied` or `NotAuthenticated` upon failure. Generic views handle this automatically.

Custom permissions inherit from `BasePermission` and can be composed using Python bitwise operators. To distinguish between read and write operations, use the `SAFE_METHODS` constant (`GET`, `OPTIONS`, `HEAD`). Custom permission classes can also define `message` and `code` attributes to customize exception details. Additionally, setting new permission classes via decorators or class attributes overrides the default settings in `settings.py`.

### IsAuthenticated¶ {#isauthenticated}

The
`IsAuthenticated`
permission class will deny permission to any unauthenticated user, and allow permission otherwise.

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to registered users.

permission class will deny permission to any user, unless

This permission is suitable if you want your API to only be accessible to a subset of trusted administrators.

`GET`
,
`HEAD`
or
`OPTIONS`
.

This permission is suitable if you want to your API to allow read permissions to anonymous users, and only allow write permissions to authenticated users.

The default behavior can also be overridden to support custom model permissions.  For example, you might want to include a
`view`

llm_response:
By default, Apache with mod_wsgi does not pass the authorization header to WSGI applications, as it assumes authentication is handled by the web server rather than the application.

To fix this, you must explicitly configure mod_wsgi to pass the required headers through to the application by adding the `WSGIPassAuthorization` directive to your server configuration, virtual host, directory, or `.htaccess` file and setting it to `'On'`:

`WSGIPassAuthorization On`

Unauthenticated requests denied permission return either an HTTP 401 Unauthorized (which must include a `WWW-Authenticate` header) or an HTTP 403 Forbidden, depending on the authentication scheme. However, a 403 response is always used if a successfully authenticated request is denied permission.

Key technical details include:
- **Middleware:** DRF views are opted-out of Django 5.1+ `LoginRequiredMiddleware`; instead, use `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`.
- **Deployment:** Apache mod_wsgi requires the `WSGIPassAuthorization On` directive to pass authorization headers.
- **SessionAuthentication:** Requires CSRF tokens for unsafe HTTP methods (PUT, PATCH, POST, DELETE).
- **Exceptions:** `NotAuthenticated` typically results in a 401 or 403 status, `PermissionDenied` results in a 403, and `NotFound` results in a 404.

### BasicAuthentication¶ {#basicauthentication}

This authentication scheme uses
HTTP Basic Authentication (https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2617)
, signed against a user's username and password.  Basic authentication is generally only appropriate for testing.

If successfully authenticated,
`BasicAuthentication`
provides the following credentials.

`request.user`
will be a Django
`User`
instance.
`request.auth`
will be
`None`
.

Unauthenticated responses that are denied permission will result in an
`HTTP 401 Unauthorized`
response with an appropriate WWW-Authenticate header.  For example:


`WWW-Authenticate:Basicrealm="api"`

The provided text outlines various authentication methods for a REST framework. Global authentication classes can be set via `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings, or configured on a per-view basis using `APIView` class-based views or the `@api_view` decorator for function-based views.

`TokenAuthentication` uses an `Authorization` header (e.g., `Token <token>`); subclassing it allows for different keywords like `Bearer`. Successful token authentication provides a Django `User` instance in `request.user` and a `Token` instance in `request.auth`. Unauthenticated requests result in an `HTTP 401 Unauthorized` response.

`RemoteUserAuthentication` delegates authentication to the web server via the `REMOTE_USER` environment variable, requiring `RemoteUserBackend` in `AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS`. It provides a `User` instance in `request.user` and sets `request.auth` to `None`. Additionally, CSRF tokens are only required for authenticated requests, except for login views.

Typically the approach you should take is:

If authentication is not attempted, return
`None`
.  Any other authentication schemes also in use will still be checked.
If authentication is attempted but fails, raise an
`AuthenticationFailed`
exception.  An error response will be returned immediately, regardless of any permissions checks, and without checking any other authentication schemes.

may

`.authenticate_header(self, request)`
method.  If implemented, it should return a string that will be used as the value of the

`HTTP 401 Unauthorized`
response.

`.authenticate_header()`
method is not overridden, the authentication scheme will return
`HTTP 403 Forbidden`
responses when an unauthenticated request is denied access.

When your custom authenticator is invoked by the request object's
`.user`
or
`.auth`
properties, you may see an
`AttributeError`
re-raised as a
`WrappedAttributeError`
. This is necessary to prevent the original exception from being suppressed by the outer property access.

user_input: I want clients to page through a huge, constantly-growing table efficiently and never see duplicates when rows are inserted mid-scroll. Which pagination style and what's the catch?
reference: CursorPagination: consistent, fixed-time paging that avoids duplicates even as rows are inserted, but it needs a unique, unchanging ordering and only allows forward/reverse navigation.
reference_contexts: Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set.
This pagination style only presents forward and reverse controls, and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions.
With extremely large datasets pagination using offset-based pagination styles may become inefficient or unusable.
The default class to use for queryset pagination.
llm_response:
To achieve efficient pagination on a huge, constantly-growing dataset while ensuring clients never see the same item twice during the process, you should use **CursorPagination**.

The catch is that this style is more complex than others and comes with specific limitations:

*   **No arbitrary navigation:** Clients are restricted to forward and reverse controls and cannot jump to specific page numbers or arbitrary positions in the dataset.
*   **Strict ordering requirements:** You must define a unique or nearly unique, unchanging, non-nullable ordering field (such as a millisecond timestamp or a slug) that is indexed in the database.
*   **Data type restrictions:** The ordering field cannot be a float, as precision errors can lead to incorrect results.
*   **Implementation effort:** While generic views and viewsets handle pagination automatically, you must manually implement it if you are using regular `APIView` classes.
llm_references:
Cursor-based pagination provides a consistent view and fixed-time performance, making it ideal for very large datasets. Unlike other schemes, it only offers forward and reverse controls and prevents clients from navigating to arbitrary positions.

To function properly, it requires a unique, unchanging, non-nullable ordering field (such as a millisecond timestamp or slug) that is indexed in the database and not a float. By default, it orders by `-created`.

Configuration can be handled globally via `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS` or per-view using the `pagination_class` attribute. The `CursorPagination` class allows overriding `page_size`, `cursor_query_param`, `ordering`, and `template`. For custom pagination styles, developers should inherit from `BasePagination` and override `paginate_queryset` and `get_paginated_response`. HTML controls can be customized by overriding specific templates or setting `template = None` to disable them.

Cursor based pagination schemes instead have fixed-time properties, and do not slow down as the dataset size increases.

#### Details and limitations¶ {#details-and-limitations}

Proper use of cursor based pagination requires a little attention to detail. You'll need to think about what ordering you want the scheme to be applied against. The default is to order by
`"-created"`
. This assumes that
there must be a 'created' timestamp field
on the model instances, and will present a "timeline" style paginated view, with the most recently added items first.

You can modify the ordering by overriding the
`'ordering'`
attribute on the pagination class, or by using the
`OrderingFilter`
filter class together with
`CursorPagination`
. When used with
`OrderingFilter`
you should strongly consider restricting the fields that the user may order by.

Proper usage of cursor pagination should have an ordering field that satisfies the following:

Should be an unchanging value, such as a timestamp, slug, or other field that is only set once, on creation.
Should be unique, or nearly unique. Millisecond precision timestamps are a good example.

This pagination style only presents forward and reverse controls, and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions.

Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set. This ordering might typically be a creation timestamp on the records, as this presents a consistent ordering to paginate against.

Cursor based pagination is more complex than other schemes. It also requires that the result set presents a fixed ordering, and does not allow the client to arbitrarily index into the result set. However it does provide the following benefits:

Provides a consistent pagination view. When used properly
`CursorPagination`
ensures that the client will never see the same item twice when paging through records, even when new items are being inserted by other clients during the pagination process.
Supports usage with very large datasets. With extremely large datasets pagination using offset-based pagination styles may become inefficient or unusable. Cursor based pagination schemes instead have fixed-time properties, and do not slow down as the dataset size increases.

#### Details and limitations¶ {#details-and-limitations}

Proper use of cursor based pagination requires a little attention to detail.

Pagination is automatically performed for generic views and viewsets, but must be manually implemented in regular `APIView` classes. It can be configured globally via `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS` and `PAGE_SIZE` settings, or on a per-view basis using the `pagination_class` attribute. Setting `pagination_class` to `None` disables pagination.

Key pagination styles include:
* **PageNumberPagination**: The default style.
* **LimitOffsetPagination**: Uses "limit" (maximum items) and "offset" (starting position) query parameters. It can be customized by overriding attributes like `default_limit`, `limit_query_param`, and `offset_query_param`.
* **CursorPagination**: Uses an opaque cursor for forward and reverse navigation, requiring a unique, unchanging ordering of items.

Additionally, generic views utilize `filter_backends` for queryset filtering and the `get_queryset()` method to determine the base queryset for list and detail views.

Pagination can be configured globally using the `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS` and `PAGE_SIZE` settings in `REST_FRAMEWORK`, or on a per-view basis using the `pagination_class` attribute. Built-in options include `LimitOffsetPagination` and `PageNumberPagination`, the latter of which uses a `page` query parameter by default.

To modify pagination behavior—such as changing the query parameter name via `page_query_param` or adjusting `max_page_size`—you must subclass the pagination class and override the desired attributes. These custom classes can then be applied globally or to specific views. 

Pagination responses typically include the total count, links to the next and previous pages, and the results. Additionally, using pagination classes automatically displays HTML pagination controls in the browsable API.

The
`pagination_serializer_class`
view attribute and
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_SERIALIZER_CLASS`
settings key
are no longer valid
. The pagination API does not use serializers to determine the output format, and you'll need to instead override the
`get_paginated_response`
method on a pagination class in order to specify how the output format is controlled.

#### New pagination schemes.¶ {#new-pagination-schemes}

Until now, there has only been a single built-in pagination style in REST framework. We now have page, limit/offset and cursor based schemes included by default.

The cursor based pagination scheme is particularly smart, and is a better approach for clients iterating through large or frequently changing result sets. The scheme supports paging against non-unique indexes, by using both cursor and limit/offset information. It also allows for both forward and reverse cursor pagination. Much credit goes to David Cramer for
this blog post (https://cra.mr/2011/03/08/building-cursors-for-the-disqus-api)
on the subject.

Should be unique, or nearly unique. Millisecond precision timestamps are a good example. This implementation of cursor pagination uses a smart "position plus offset" style that allows it to properly support not-strictly-unique values as the ordering.
Should be a non-nullable value that can be coerced to a string.
Should not be a float. Precision errors easily lead to incorrect results.
Hint: use decimals instead.
(If you already have a float field and must paginate on that, an
example CursorPagination subclass that uses decimals to limit precision is available here (https://gist.github.com/keturn/8bc88525a183fd41c73ffb729b8865be#file-fpcursorpagination-py)
.)
The field should have a database index.

Using an ordering field that does not satisfy these constraints will generally still work, but you'll be losing some of the benefits of cursor pagination.

For more technical details on the implementation we use for cursor pagination, the
"Building cursors for the Disqus API" (https://cra.mr/2011/03/08/building-cursors-for-the-disqus-api)
blog post gives a good overview of the basic approach.

To achieve rich, declarative filtering on multiple model fields, you can use the `django-filter` library. Additionally, there are several third-party packages that integrate with the framework to provide extended filtering capabilities:

*   **drf-url-filters**: A simple app designed to apply filters on a `ModelViewSet`'s queryset. It supports validation of incoming query parameters and their values using the `Voluptuous` library, allowing you to define custom validation requirements.

### SearchFilter¶ {#searchfilter}

The
`SearchFilter`
class supports simple single query parameter based searching, and is based on the
Django admin's search functionality (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/contrib/admin/#django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin.search_fields)
.

When in use, the browsable API will include a
`SearchFilter`
control:

The

`search_fields`

or

.

`fromrest_frameworkimportfiltersclassUserListView(generics.ListAPIView):queryset=User.objects.all()serializer_class=UserSerializerfilter_backends=[filters.SearchFilter]search_fields=['username','email']`


This will allow the client to filter the items in the list by making queries such as:


`http://example.com/api/users?search=russell`


You can also perform a related lookup on a ForeignKey or ManyToManyField with the lookup API double-underscore notation:


`search_fields=['username','email','profile__profession']`


For
JSONField (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/models/fields/#django.db.models.JSONField)
and
HStoreField (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/contrib/postgres/fields/#hstorefield)
fields you can filter based on nested values within the data structure using the same double-underscore notation:


`search_fields=['data__breed','data__owner__other_pets__0__name']`

REST framework provides several ways to filter querysets. You can override `.get_queryset()` to filter based on the currently authenticated user (`request.user`), specific URL components (using `self.kwargs`), or query parameters (`self.request.query_params`).

Additionally, the framework supports generic filtering backends for complex searches, which can be configured globally via the `DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS` setting or on a per-view/viewset basis using `GenericAPIView`. The `django-filter` library offers the `DjangoFilterBackend` class for highly customizable field filtering. 

Notably, an overridden `.get_queryset()` method can be used in conjunction with generic filtering to first restrict the initial queryset and then apply further filters.

Django REST framework offers multiple ways to filter and order querysets. The simplest method is overriding `get_queryset()` to filter by authenticated users, URL components, or query parameters. For advanced needs, `django-filter` provides `DjangoFilterBackend` for customizable field filtering via `filterset_fields`.

The `SearchFilter` class enables case-insensitive partial matches using `search_fields`, supporting related lookups and specific prefixes for exact, starts-with, regex, or full-text searches. `OrderingFilter` allows result ordering via query parameters. 

Developers can implement custom filter backends, such as `IsOwnerFilterBackend` for scalability, or create mixins like `MultipleFieldLookupMixin` for complex object lookups. Global configurations are managed via `DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS`. Additionally, third-party packages like `django-rest-framework-filters` and `drf-url-filters` extend functionality for relationship and URL filtering. Filter backends apply to both list views and single object lookups.

You can also set the filter backends on a per-view, or per-viewset basis,
using the
`GenericAPIView`
class-based views.


`importdjango_filters.rest_frameworkfromdjango.contrib.auth.modelsimportUserfrommyapp.serializersimportUserSerializerfromrest_frameworkimportgenericsclassUserListView(generics.ListAPIView):queryset=User.objects.all()serializer_class=UserSerializerfilter_backends=[django_filters.rest_framework.DjangoFilterBackend]`


### Filtering and object lookups¶ {#filtering-and-object-lookups}

Note that if a filter backend is configured for a view, then as well as being used to filter list views, it will also be used to filter the querysets used for returning a single object.

For instance, given the previous example, and a product with an id of
`4675`
, the following URL would either return the corresponding object, or return a 404 response, depending on if the filtering conditions were met by the given product instance:


`http://example.com/api/products/4675/?category=clothing&max_price=10.00`

Django REST framework allows you to restrict the items returned by generic list views. The simplest method is overriding the `.get_queryset()` method of `GenericAPIView`, which is useful for filtering results based on the currently authenticated user.

For more advanced filtering, you can use `django-filter` by installing the package, adding `'django_filters'` to `INSTALLED_APPS`, and configuring `DjangoFilterBackend` globally in settings or on a per-view basis. Simple equality-based filtering is achieved by defining a `filterset_fields` attribute.

Additionally, `filters.SearchFilter` enables search functionality via `search_fields`. This supports related lookups on ForeignKey or ManyToManyFields, as well as nested values in `JSONField` and `HStoreField`, using double-underscore notation. Note that configured filter backends apply to both list views and single object lookups, potentially resulting in a 404 response if filtering conditions are not met.

user_input: I want to stop a user creating two records with the same combination of two fields — like no two items sharing a position in the same list. How do I express that in DRF validation?
reference: Apply a UniqueTogetherValidator in the serializer's Meta.validators with the queryset and the field names that must be unique as a set; note it implicitly treats those fields as required.
reference_contexts: This validator can be used to enforce unique_together constraints on model instances.
fields required - A list or tuple of field names which should make a unique set.
all (), fields =[ 'list' , 'position' ] ) ] Note The UniqueTogetherValidator class always imposes an implicit constraint that all the fields it applies to are always treated as required.
Serializer classes can also include reusable validators that are applied to the complete set of field data.
llm_response:
To enforce a constraint where a combination of two fields must be unique, you should use the `UniqueTogetherValidator`. This validator is applied to the serializer class within the `Meta` options.

You must provide the `queryset` against which the uniqueness should be enforced and a list of the `fields` that make up the unique set.

Here is an example of how to implement it:

```python
from rest_framework.validators import UniqueTogetherValidator

class ExampleSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    # ... fields ...

    class Meta:
        # ...
        validators = [
            UniqueTogetherValidator(
                queryset=ToDoItem.objects.all(),
                fields=['list', 'position']
            )
        ]
```

Note that this validator implicitly treats the specified fields as required unless they have default values. If you need to make one of these fields optional, you will need to exclude the validator and handle the validation logic explicitly in the `.validate()` method or in the view.
llm_references: `classBillingRecordSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):defvalidate(self,attrs):# Apply custom validation either here, or in the view.classMeta:fields=['client','date','amount']extra_kwargs={'client':{'required':False}}validators=[]# Remove a default "unique together" constraint.`

The interesting bit here is the
`reference`
field. We can see that the uniqueness constraint is being explicitly enforced by a validator on the serializer field.

Because of this more explicit style REST framework includes a few validator classes that are not available in core Django. These classes are detailed below.  REST framework validators, like their Django counterparts, implement the
`__eq__`
method, allowing you to compare instances for equality.

## UniqueValidator¶ {#uniquevalidator}

This validator can be used to enforce the
`unique=True`
constraint on model fields.
It takes a single required argument, and an optional
`messages`
argument:

`queryset`
required
- This is the queryset against which uniqueness should be enforced.
`message`
- The error message that should be used when validation fails.
`lookup`
- The lookup used to find an existing instance with the value being validated. Defaults to
`'exact'`
.

This validator should be applied to
serializer fields
, like so:


`fromrest_framework.validatorsimportUniqueValidatorslug=SlugField(max_length=100,validators=[UniqueValidator(queryset=BlogPost.objects.all())])`

`fromrest_framework.validatorsimportUniqueValidatorslug=SlugField(max_length=100,validators=[UniqueValidator(queryset=BlogPost.objects.all())])`


## UniqueTogetherValidator¶ {#uniquetogethervalidator}

This validator can be used to enforce
`unique_together`
constraints on model instances.
It has two required arguments, and a single optional
`messages`
argument:

`queryset`
required
- This is the queryset against which uniqueness should be enforced.
`fields`
required
- A list or tuple of field names which should make a unique set. These must exist as fields on the serializer class.
`message`
- The error message that should be used when validation fails.

The validator should be applied to
serializer classes
, like so:


`fromrest_framework.validatorsimportUniqueTogetherValidatorclassExampleSerializer(serializers.Serializer):# ...classMeta:# ToDo items belong to a parent list, and have an ordering defined# by the 'position' field. No two items in a given list may share# the same position.validators=[UniqueTogetherValidator(queryset=ToDoItem.objects.all(),fields=['list','position'])]`

But we also get the built-in validation for free:


`>>>invalid_data={..."label":"still testing",..."coordinates":{..."x":'a',..."y":'b',...}...}>>>invalid_serializer=DataPointSerializer(data=invalid_data)>>>invalid_serializer.is_valid()False>>>invalid_serializer.errorsReturnDict([('coordinates',{'x':['A valid integer is required.'],'y':['A valid integer is required.']})])`


For this reason, the nested serializer approach would be the first to try. You
would use the custom field approach when the nested serializer becomes infeasible
or overly complex.

## Third party packages¶ {#third-party-packages}

The following third party packages are also available.

### DRF Compound Fields¶ {#drf-compound-fields}

The
drf-compound-fields (https://drf-compound-fields.readthedocs.io)
package provides "compound" serializer fields, such as lists of simple values, which can be described by other fields rather than serializers with the
`many=True`
option. Also provided are fields for typed dictionaries and values that can be either a specific type or a list of items of that type.

`created_at=serializers.DateTimeField(default=serializers.CreateOnlyDefault(timezone.now))`


## Limitations of validators¶ {#limitations-of-validators}

There are some ambiguous cases where you'll need to instead handle validation
explicitly, rather than relying on the default serializer classes that
`ModelSerializer`
generates.

In these cases you may want to disable the automatically generated validators,
by specifying an empty list for the serializer
`Meta.validators`
attribute.

### Optional fields¶ {#optional-fields}

By default "unique together" validation enforces that all fields be
`required=True`
. In some cases, you might want to explicit apply
`required=False`
to one of the fields, in which case the desired behavior
of the validation is ambiguous.

In this case you will typically need to exclude the validator from the
serializer class, and instead write any validation logic explicitly, either
in the
`.validate()`
method, or else in the view.

For example:

Note
There is a special-case where a read-only field is part of a
`unique_together`
constraint at the model level. In this case the field is required by the serializer class in order to validate the constraint, but should also not be editable by the user.
The right way to deal with this is to specify the field explicitly on the serializer, providing both the
`read_only=True`
and
`default=…`
keyword arguments.
One example of this is a read-only relation to the currently authenticated
`User`
which is
`unique_together`
with another identifier. In this case you would declare the user field like so:

`user=serializers.PrimaryKeyRelatedField(read_only=True,default=serializers.CurrentUserDefault())`

Please review the
Validators Documentation (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/validators/)
for details on the
UniqueTogetherValidator (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/validators/#uniquetogethervalidator)
and
CurrentUserDefault (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/validators/#currentuserdefault)
classes.

REST framework provides several validator classes to enforce uniqueness constraints on serializer fields and classes:

*   **UniqueValidator**: Enforces `unique=True` on serializer fields using a required `queryset`, an optional `message`, and a `lookup` (defaults to 'exact').
*   **UniqueTogetherValidator**: Enforces `unique_together` constraints on serializer classes. It requires a `queryset` and a list of `fields`. It implicitly treats these fields as required unless they have default values.
*   **UniqueForDate/Month/YearValidator**: Enforce date-range uniqueness on serializer classes, requiring a `queryset`, a `field`, and a `date_field`.

During updates, uniqueness validators exclude the current instance. However, this exclusion is not possible for nested serializers, requiring manual validation in the view or `.validate()` method. To debug automatically generated validators in `ModelSerializer`, users can inspect a serializer instance via `manage.py shell`.

Otherwise the default_detail attribute from PermissionDenied will be used.
llm_response: To provide a custom, human-friendly denial message for your permission, implement a `message` attribute directly on your custom permission class. If this attribute is not defined, the system will default to the `default_detail` attribute from the `PermissionDenied` exception.
