For example:


`ifrequest.methodinpermissions.SAFE_METHODS:# Check permissions for read-only requestelse:# Check permissions for write request`


Note
The instance-level
`has_object_permission`
method will only be called if the view-level
`has_permission`
checks have already passed. Also note that in order for the instance-level checks to run, the view code should explicitly call
`.check_object_permissions(request, obj)`
. If you are using the generic views then this will be handled for you by default. (Function-based views will need to check object permissions explicitly, raising
`PermissionDenied`
on failure.)

Custom permissions will raise a
`PermissionDenied`
exception if the test fails. To change the error message associated with the exception, implement a
`message`
attribute directly on your custom permission. Otherwise the
`default_detail`
attribute from
`PermissionDenied`

attribute from

will be used.

The provided text explains how to implement and manage permissions in a REST framework. Global permissions are checked against all requests, while object-level permissions apply to specific object instances. To enforce object-level permissions in custom views or overridden `get_object` methods, you must explicitly call `.check_object_permissions(request, obj)`, which raises `PermissionDenied` or `NotAuthenticated` upon failure. Generic views handle this automatically.

Custom permissions inherit from `BasePermission` and can be composed using Python bitwise operators. To distinguish between read and write operations, use the `SAFE_METHODS` constant (`GET`, `OPTIONS`, `HEAD`). Custom permission classes can also define `message` and `code` attributes to customize exception details. Additionally, setting new permission classes via decorators or class attributes overrides the default settings in `settings.py`.

The provided text outlines access restriction methods and third-party packages for API permissions. Core methods include `permission_classes`/`get_permissions()` for general and object-level checks, `serializer_class`/`get_serializer()` for instance-level restrictions, and `queryset` for global control. The `get_*()` methods allow for dynamic returns based on the request or action.

Several third-party packages extend these capabilities:
- **Complex Rules:** DRF - Access Policy (JSON-based), Composed Permissions, and REST Condition (logical operators).
- **Role/User Management:** Django Rest Framework Roles, Rest Framework Roles, and Django Rest Framework Role Filters.
- **Specialized Access:** DRY Rest Permissions (relationship-derived permissions), Django REST Framework API Key (machine authorization), Django Rest Framework PSQ (permission-based rules), and Axioms DRF PY (claim-based authorization via JWT/OAuth2).

As with
`DjangoModelPermissions`
you can use custom model permissions by overriding
`DjangoObjectPermissions`
and setting the
`.perms_map`
property.  Refer to the source code for details.

Note
If you need object level
`view`
permissions for
`GET`
,
`HEAD`
and
`OPTIONS`
requests and are using django-guardian for your object-level permissions backend, you'll want to consider using the
`DjangoObjectPermissionsFilter`
class provided by the
djangorestframework-guardian package (https://github.com/rpkilby/django-rest-framework-guardian)
. It ensures that list endpoints only return results including objects for which the user has appropriate view permissions.

## Custom permissions¶ {#custom-permissions}

To implement a custom permission, override
`BasePermission`
and implement either, or both, of the following methods:

`.has_permission(self, request, view)`
`.has_object_permission(self, request, view, obj)`

The methods should return
`True`
if the request should be granted access, and
`False`
otherwise.

The extension allows you to combine permissions with logical operators.

### DRY Rest Permissions¶ {#dry-rest-permissions}

The
DRY Rest Permissions (https://github.com/FJNR-inc/dry-rest-permissions)
package provides the ability to define different permissions for individual default and custom actions. This package is made for apps with permissions that are derived from relationships defined in the app's data model. It also supports permission checks being returned to a client app through the API's serializer. Additionally it supports adding permissions to the default and custom list actions to restrict the data they retrieve per user.

### Django Rest Framework Roles¶ {#django-rest-framework-roles}

The
Django Rest Framework Roles (https://github.com/computer-lab/django-rest-framework-roles)
package makes it easier to parameterize your API over multiple types of users.

### Rest Framework Roles¶ {#rest-framework-roles}

The
Rest Framework Roles (https://github.com/Pithikos/rest-framework-roles)
makes it super easy to protect views based on roles. Most importantly allows you to decouple accessibility logic from models and views in a clean human-readable way.

The default behavior can also be overridden to support custom model permissions.  For example, you might want to include a
`view`
model permission for
`GET`
requests.

To use custom model permissions, override
`DjangoModelPermissions`
and set the
`.perms_map`
property.  Refer to the source code for details.

### DjangoModelPermissionsOrAnonReadOnly¶ {#djangomodelpermissionsoranonreadonly}

Similar to
`DjangoModelPermissions`
, but also allows unauthenticated users to have read-only access to the API.

### DjangoObjectPermissions¶ {#djangoobjectpermissions}

This permission class ties into Django's standard
object permissions framework (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/auth/customizing/#handling-object-permissions)
that allows per-object permissions on models.  In order to use this permission class, you'll also need to add a permission backend that supports object-level permissions, such as
django-guardian (https://github.com/lukaszb/django-guardian)
.

As with
`DjangoModelPermissions`
, this permission must only be applied to views that have a
`.queryset`
property or
`.get_queryset()`
method.

## Third party packages¶ {#third-party-packages}

The following third party packages are also available.

### DRF - Access Policy¶ {#drf-access-policy}

The
Django REST - Access Policy (https://github.com/rsinger86/drf-access-policy)
package provides a way to define complex access rules in declarative policy classes that are attached to view sets or function-based views. The policies are defined in JSON in a format similar to AWS' Identity & Access Management policies.

### Composed Permissions¶ {#composed-permissions}

The
Composed Permissions (https://github.com/niwibe/djangorestframework-composed-permissions)
package provides a simple way to define complex and multi-depth (with logic operators) permission objects, using small and reusable components.

### REST Condition¶ {#rest-condition}

The
REST Condition (https://github.com/caxap/rest_condition)
package is another extension for building complex permissions in a simple and convenient way. The extension allows you to combine permissions with logical operators.

user_input: When should I reach for a ReadOnlyModelViewSet instead of a full ModelViewSet, and what do the two actually differ on?
reference: Use ReadOnlyModelViewSet when you only need read endpoints: it provides just .list() and .retrieve(), whereas ModelViewSet gives the full create/list/retrieve/update/destroy set. Both inherit from GenericAPIView and both still require queryset and serializer_class.
reference_contexts: all () serializer_class = UserSerializer Here we've used the ReadOnlyModelViewSet class to automatically provide the default 'read-only' operations.
We're still setting the queryset and serializer_class attributes exactly as we did when we were using regular views, but we no longer need to provide the same information to two separate classes.
The ModelViewSet class inherits from GenericAPIView and includes implementations for various actions, by mixing in the behavior of the various mixin classes.
The ReadOnlyModelViewSet class also inherits from GenericAPIView .
llm_response:
You should use a `ReadOnlyModelViewSet` when you want to provide access to data without allowing users to create, update, or delete instances. 

The primary difference between the two is the set of actions they provide:

*   **`ModelViewSet`**: Includes the full set of operations, specifically `.list()`, `.retrieve()`, `.create()`, `.update()`, `.partial_update()`, and `.destroy()`.
*   **`ReadOnlyModelViewSet`**: Includes only the read-only operations, which are limited to `.list()` and `.retrieve()`.

Both classes inherit from `GenericAPIView` and typically require the same `queryset` and `serializer_class` attributes to function.
llm_references:
The provided text explains different types of ViewSet classes. `GenericViewSet` requires overriding the class to either mix in required mixin classes or define action implementations explicitly. 

`ModelViewSet` inherits from `GenericAPIView` and provides a full set of actions: `.list()`, `.retrieve()`, `.create()`, `.update()`, `.partial_update()`, and `.destroy()`. `ReadOnlyModelViewSet` similarly inherits from `GenericAPIView` but only provides the read-only actions `.list()` and `.retrieve()`. Both typically require `queryset` and `serializer_class` attributes, though `get_queryset()` can be used for dynamic determination. If the `queryset` property is removed, the `basename` kwarg must be specified during router registration.

Additionally, custom ViewSet base classes can be created by inheriting from `GenericViewSet` and mixing in specific actions, such as combining `CreateModelMixin`, `ListModelMixin`, and `RetrieveModelMixin` to provide only create, list, and retrieve operations.

In order to use a
`GenericViewSet`
class you'll override the class and either mixin the required mixin classes, or define the action implementations explicitly.

### ModelViewSet¶ {#modelviewset}

The
`ModelViewSet`
class inherits from
`GenericAPIView`
and includes implementations for various actions, by mixing in the behavior of the various mixin classes.

The actions provided by the
`ModelViewSet`
class are
`.list()`
,
`.retrieve()`
,
`.create()`
,
`.update()`
,
`.partial_update()`
, and
`.destroy()`
.

#### Example¶ {#example_1}

Because
`ModelViewSet`
extends
`GenericAPIView`
, you'll normally need to provide at least the
`queryset`
and
`serializer_class`
attributes.  For example:


`classAccountViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):"""
A simple ViewSet for viewing and editing accounts.
"""queryset=Account.objects.all()serializer_class=AccountSerializerpermission_classes=[IsAccountAdminOrReadOnly]`

`classAccountViewSet(viewsets.ReadOnlyModelViewSet):"""
A simple ViewSet for viewing accounts.
"""queryset=Account.objects.all()serializer_class=AccountSerializer`


Again, as with
`ModelViewSet`
, you can use any of the standard attributes and method overrides available to
`GenericAPIView`
.

## Custom ViewSet base classes¶ {#custom-viewset-base-classes}

You may need to provide custom
`ViewSet`
classes that do not have the full set of
`ModelViewSet`
actions, or that customize the behavior in some other way.

### Example¶ {#example_3}

`create`
,
`list`
and
`retrieve`

A viewset that provides `retrieve`, `create`, and `list` actions.

## Refactoring to use ViewSets¶ {#refactoring-to-use-viewsets}

Let's take our current set of views, and refactor them into view sets.

First of all let's refactor our
`UserList`
and
`UserDetail`
classes into a single
`UserViewSet`
class. In the
`snippets/views.py`
file, we can remove the two view classes and replace them with a single ViewSet class:


`fromrest_frameworkimportviewsetsclassUserViewSet(viewsets.ReadOnlyModelViewSet):"""This viewset automatically provides `list` and `retrieve` actions."""queryset=User.objects.all()serializer_class=UserSerializer`


Here we've used the
`ReadOnlyModelViewSet`
class to automatically provide the default 'read-only' operations.  We're still setting the
`queryset`
and
`serializer_class`
attributes exactly as we did when we were using regular views, but we no longer need to provide the same information to two separate classes.

Next we're going to replace the
`SnippetList`
,
`SnippetDetail`
and
`SnippetHighlight`
view classes.  We can remove the three views, and again replace them with a single class.

For example:


`classAccountViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):"""
A simple ViewSet for viewing and editing accounts.
"""queryset=Account.objects.all()serializer_class=AccountSerializerpermission_classes=[IsAccountAdminOrReadOnly]`


Note that you can use any of the standard attributes or method overrides provided by
`GenericAPIView`
.  For example, to use a
`ViewSet`
that dynamically determines the queryset it should operate on, you might do something like this:


`classAccountViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):"""
A simple ViewSet for viewing and editing the accounts
associated with the user.
"""serializer_class=AccountSerializerpermission_classes=[IsAccountAdminOrReadOnly]defget_queryset(self):returnself.request.user.accounts.all()`

Note however that upon removal of the
`queryset`
property from your
`ViewSet`
, any associated
router (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/routers/)
will be unable to derive the basename of your Model automatically, and so you will have to specify the
`basename`
kwarg as part of your
router registration (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/routers/)
.

Also note that although this class provides the complete set of create/list/retrieve/update/destroy actions by default, you can restrict the available operations by using the standard permission classes.

### ReadOnlyModelViewSet¶ {#readonlymodelviewset}

The
`ReadOnlyModelViewSet`
class also inherits from
`GenericAPIView`
.  As with
`ModelViewSet`
it also includes implementations for various actions, but unlike
`ModelViewSet`
only provides the 'read-only' actions,
`.list()`
and
`.retrieve()`
.

#### Example¶ {#example_2}

As with
`ModelViewSet`
, you'll normally need to provide at least the
`queryset`
and
`serializer_class`
attributes.  For example:

`classUserViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):"""
A viewset for viewing and editing user instances.
"""serializer_class=UserSerializerqueryset=User.objects.all()`


There are two main advantages of using a
`ViewSet`
class over using a
`View`
class.

Repeated logic can be combined into a single class.  In the above example, we only need to specify the
`queryset`
once, and it'll be used across multiple views.
By using routers, we no longer need to deal with wiring up the URL conf ourselves.

Both of these come with a trade-off.  Using regular views and URL confs is more explicit and gives you more control.  ViewSets are helpful if you want to get up and running quickly, or when you have a large API and you want to enforce a consistent URL configuration throughout.

The provided text explains how to implement and manage permissions in a REST framework. Global permissions are checked against all requests, while object-level permissions apply to specific object instances. To enforce object-level permissions in custom views or overridden `get_object` methods, you must explicitly call `.check_object_permissions(request, obj)`, which raises `PermissionDenied` or `NotAuthenticated` upon failure. Generic views handle this automatically.

Custom permissions inherit from `BasePermission` and can be composed using Python bitwise operators. To distinguish between read and write operations, use the `SAFE_METHODS` constant (`GET`, `OPTIONS`, `HEAD`). Custom permission classes can also define `message` and `code` attributes to customize exception details. Additionally, setting new permission classes via decorators or class attributes overrides the default settings in `settings.py`.

Whether an unauthenticated request receives a 401 Unauthorized or a 403 Forbidden response depends on the authentication scheme being used.

The determination is made based on the highest priority authentication class set on the view:

*   **401 Unauthorized:** This response is returned if the authentication scheme uses `WWW-Authenticate` headers. When this occurs, the response must include a `WWW-Authenticate` header to instruct the client on how to authenticate.

If you are implementing a custom authenticator, you can control this behavior by overriding the `.authenticate_header(self, request)` method. If this method is implemented and returns a string, the system will return a 401 response with that string as the header value. If the method is not overridden, the authentication scheme will default to returning a 403 response for unauthenticated requests that are denied access.

## Object level permissions¶ {#object-level-permissions}

REST framework permissions also support object-level permissioning.  Object level permissions are used to determine if a user should be allowed to act on a particular object, which will typically be a model instance.

Object level permissions are run by REST framework's generic views when

The provided text outlines authentication and error handling in the Django REST framework (DRF). Unauthenticated requests denied permission return either an HTTP 401 Unauthorized (which must include a `WWW-Authenticate` header) or an HTTP 403 Forbidden, depending on the authentication scheme. However, a 403 response is always used if a successfully authenticated request is denied permission.

Key technical details include:
- **Middleware:** DRF views are opted-out of Django 5.1+ `LoginRequiredMiddleware`; instead, use `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`.
- **Deployment:** Apache mod_wsgi requires the `WSGIPassAuthorization On` directive to pass authorization headers.
- **SessionAuthentication:** Requires CSRF tokens for unsafe HTTP methods (PUT, PATCH, POST, DELETE).
- **Exceptions:** `NotAuthenticated` typically results in a 401 or 403 status, `PermissionDenied` results in a 403, and `NotFound` results in a 404.

See the
authentication documentation (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/)
for more details.

The simplest style of permission would be to allow access to any authenticated user, and deny access to any unauthenticated user. This corresponds to the

Before running the main body of the view each permission in the list is checked.

or
`exceptions.NotAuthenticated`
exception will be raised, and the main body of the view will not run.

When the permission checks fail, either a "403 Forbidden" or a "401 Unauthorized" response will be returned, according to the following rules:

The request was successfully authenticated, but permission was denied.

Django REST framework runs object-level permission checks only when the `has_object_permission()` method is invoked. In generic views, this happens automatically for detail endpoints because they call `get_object()` and subsequently trigger `.check_object_permissions(request, obj)`.

However, object-level checks are not automatically applied in the following scenarios:
* **List views:** For performance reasons, generic views do not run object-level checks on every instance in a queryset.
* **Object creation:** The `get_object()` method is not called during creation, so object-level permissions are not applied.
* **Custom views:** If you are not using generic views, the framework does not automatically trigger these checks.

**What to do in your own view:**
If you are writing a custom view or overriding the `get_object()` method, you must explicitly call `.check_object_permissions(request, obj)` once you have retrieved the object instance. This method will either return if the user is authorized or raise a `PermissionDenied` or `NotAuthenticated` exception if the check fails.

Additionally, keep in mind that:
* The `has_object_permission()` method is only executed if the view-level `has_permission()` checks have already passed.
* Most built-in permission classes do not implement object-level checks (with the exception of `DjangoObjectPermissions`). If you want to use standard permission classes for object-level checks, you must subclass them and implement the `has_object_permission()` method yourself.
* To restrict visibility for list views or object creation, you should filter the `queryset` or override `get_queryset()` rather than relying on object-level permission checks.

The choice between these three methods depends on the level of control required and the specific action being performed.

### **Queryset**
*   **List:** Provides global control by filtering the data returned to the user. It is the primary way to restrict visibility for list actions.
*   **Create:** Does not provide control over the creation process.

### **Permission Classes (`permission_classes` / `get_permissions`)**
*   **List:** Offers global control over whether a user is allowed to access the list view at all.
*   **Create:** Offers global control over whether a user is permitted to perform the creation action.
*   **General:** These are best for checking the current action, the request, and the targeted object. While they can handle object-level permissions for retrieve, update, and delete actions, they apply to the entire object type for list and create actions.

### **Serializer (`serializer_class` / `get_serializer`)**
*   **List:** Offers instance-level restrictions on the output. Note that a serializer should not raise `PermissionDenied` during a list action, as this would prevent the entire list from being returned.
*   **Create:** Offers instance-level restrictions on the input. This is a common place to enforce checks during object creation, as `get_object()` is not called for creation actions.
*   **General:** These provide instance-level restrictions that apply to all objects on both input and output. Because `get_serializer()` has access to the request context, it can return different serializers based on the current action.

### **Summary Table for List vs. Create**

| Method | Action: List | Action: Create |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Queryset** | Global control | No control |
| **Permission Classes** | Global control | Global control |
| **Serializer** | Object-level* | Object-level |

*\*Serializers should not raise `PermissionDenied` during list actions.*

To build a cohesive API where snippets have owners, support public read access, and restrict write/delete operations to the owner, you should utilize the following components:

### 1. Permissions
Implement `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly` to allow public read access while requiring authentication for writes. To ensure only the creator can modify or delete a snippet, use a custom `IsOwnerOrReadOnly` permission class.

### 2. Serializers
Use a `ModelSerializer` (or `HyperlinkedModelSerializer` for better discoverability) to handle data conversion. Include a `ReadOnlyField` in your `SnippetSerializer` with `source="owner.username"` to display the creator's username without allowing it to be modified during deserialization.

### 3. ViewSets and Logic
Instead of standard class-based views, use a `ViewSet`. This allows you to group the logic for your snippets into a single class. To associate the user with the snippet, override the `.perform_create()` method within your view logic:
```python
def perform_create(self, serializer):
    serializer.save(owner=self.request.user)
```

### 4. Routers
To avoid manually writing every URL entry, use a `Router`. By registering your `ViewSet` with a `DefaultRouter`, the framework will automatically generate the URL patterns for your list and detail routes. 

### How they fit together:
*   **The ViewSet** handles the request logic and applies the permission classes.
*   **The Serializer** manages the data representation, ensuring the `owner` field is read-only and correctly mapped to the user.
*   **The Router** inspects the `ViewSet` and automatically maps the appropriate HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to the corresponding actions, eliminating the need for manual `urls.py` configuration for every route. 

By binding these together, you create a clean, automated, and secure API structure that handles user association and access control consistently.

reference: They're separate but sequential: authentication identifies the request and runs first (setting request.user/request.auth), then permissions use that to allow or deny. Set authentication_classes and permission_classes together — authentication alone never grants access.

llm_response:
To control authentication and permissions on a per-view basis, you can define the `authentication_classes` and `permission_classes` attributes directly within your `APIView` class. 

When a request is made to an `APIView`, the system will first authenticate the request using the specified authentication schemes and then perform the permission checks before dispatching the request to the appropriate handler method (such as `.get()` or `.post()`).

You can set both on a single `APIView` as shown in this example:

```python
from rest_framework.authentication import SessionAuthentication, BasicAuthentication
from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated
from rest_framework.response import Response
from rest_framework.views import APIView

class ExampleView(APIView):
    # Define the authentication schemes
    authentication_classes = [SessionAuthentication, BasicAuthentication]
    
    # Define the permission policies
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

    def get(self, request, format=None):
        content = {
            'user': str(request.user),
            'auth': str(request.auth),
        }
        return Response(content)
```

In this configuration, the view will require the user to be authenticated via either Session or Basic authentication, and the `IsAuthenticated` permission will ensure that only registered users can access the endpoint.

reference: Any relational serialization can trigger a hit per object, so it's the programmer's job to optimize queries (e.g. prefetch). The same applies to source when it walks a relational ORM attribute — a known N+1 risk to prefetch around.
reference_contexts: It is the programmer's responsibility to optimize queries to avoid additional database hits which could occur while using such a serializer.
For example, the following serializer would lead to a database hit each time evaluating the tracks field if it is not prefetched: class AlbumSerializer ( serializers .
Beware of possible n+1 problems when using source attribute if you are accessing a relational orm model.
llm_response:
You should worry about N+1 queries whenever a serializer accesses related objects that have not been pre-fetched. This occurs in two primary scenarios:

*   **Using the `source` argument:** When you use dotted notation (e.g., `source="user.email"`) to traverse a relational model, the system may trigger a database hit for each item to fetch the related object if it is not already in memory.
*   **Using relational fields:** When a serializer field spans an ORM relation, it may require an additional database hit to fetch the related data for every instance in a queryset. This is particularly problematic when serializing a large queryset with `many=True`.

To prevent these performance issues, you must manually optimize your querysets in `get_queryset()` or by setting the `queryset` attribute on your view. Use `select_related()` for `ForeignKey` and `OneToOneField` relationships, and `prefetch_related()` for reverse and many-to-many relationships.
llm_references:
Generally we recommend a flat style for API representations where possible, but the nested URL style can also be reasonable when used in moderation.

This is achieved by overriding the `.to_representation()` method, which can return a simple textual representation or a nested representation using specific serializers based on the instance type. Conversely, reverse generic keys using `GenericRelation` can be serialized with regular relational field types because the target type is known. The provided text explains how to handle relational fields in the Django REST Framework. Key points include:

*   **Optimization:** REST Framework does not automatically optimize querysets. Programmers must use `select_related` or `prefetch_related` to avoid performance issues caused by additional database hits when serializing relations.
*   **Relational Fields:** Various fields are available for representing relationships, such as `StringRelatedField` (using `__str__`), `HyperlinkedIdentityField` (read-only URLs), and custom `RelatedField` subclasses for specific representations.
*   **Nested Serializers:** Serializers can be used as fields to create nested representations. While read-only by default, they can be made writable by implementing `create()` and `update()` methods.
*   **Inspection:** Automatically generated fields in a `ModelSerializer` can be inspected by printing the object representation of the serializer instance in the Django shell.

Serializer field constructors accept several core arguments:

*   **read_only**: If `True`, the field is included in output but ignored during create/update operations.
*   **write_only**: If `True`, the field is used for create/update but excluded from output.
*   **required**: Defaults to `True`. If `False`, the field is not mandatory during deserialization and may be omitted from output.
*   **default**: Provides a value if none is supplied. It can be a callable and implies the field is not required; using both `default` and `required` raises an error.
*   **allow_null**: If `True`, `None` is a valid value.
*   **source**: Specifies the attribute used to populate the field. It supports methods, dotted notation for traversal, or `'*'` to pass the entire object. Dotted notation may require a `default` and can cause n+1 database problems if not handled with `select_related` or `prefetch_related`.

user_input: I want to hand out one auth token per user automatically at account creation, and also backfill tokens for existing users. What's the pattern for both?
reference: For new users, catch the user post_save signal and Token.objects.create(user=instance) when created; for existing users, loop User.objects.all() and Token.objects.get_or_create(user=user).
reference_contexts: If you want every user to have an automatically generated Token, you can simply catch the User's post_save signal.
If you've already created some users, you can generate tokens for all existing users like this: from django .
create ( user = instance ) Note that you'll want to ensure you place this code snippet in an installed models.py module, or some other location that will be imported by Django on startup.
A list or tuple of authentication classes, that determines the default set of authenticators used when accessing the request.user or request.auth properties.
llm_response:
To automatically generate a token for every user upon account creation, you can use a Django `post_save` signal. Place the following code in an installed `models.py` module or another location that is imported by Django on startup:

```python
from django.conf import settings
from django.db.models.signals import post_save
from django.dispatch import receiver
from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token

@receiver(post_save, sender=settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL)
def create_auth_token(sender, instance=None, created=False, **kwargs):
    if created:
        Token.objects.create(user=instance)
```

To backfill tokens for users that were created before implementing the signal, you can run the following script:

```python
from django.contrib.auth.models import User
from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token

for user in User.objects.all():
    Token.objects.get_or_create(user=user)
```

The authentication schemes are always defined as a list of classes.  REST framework will attempt to authenticate with each class in the list, and will set

user_input: How does DRF's Request relate to the parsers, and what does request.data give me that request.POST doesn't?
reference: request.data is DRF's flexible replacement for request.POST: it handles arbitrary parsed content for POST, PUT and PATCH, not just form data. The parser classes DRF selects do the actual parsing, so request.data works across formats like JSON.
reference_contexts: The core functionality of the Request object is the request.data attribute, which is similar to request.POST , but more useful for working with Web APIs.
request.data can handle incoming json requests, but it can also handle other formats.

The wrappers also provide behavior such as returning 405 Method Not Allowed responses when appropriate, and handling any ParseError exceptions that occur when accessing request.data with malformed input.
request.data will be populated with a dictionary of data.
request.query_params is a more correctly named synonym for request.GET .
llm_response:
The `Request` object in the REST framework utilizes Parser classes to process incoming request bodies. When `request.data` is accessed, the framework examines the `Content-Type` header of the incoming request to determine which parser to use. These parsers can be configured globally via `DEFAULT_PARSER_CLASSES` or specifically for individual views using the `parser_classes` attribute or the `@parser_classes` decorator.

Compared to the standard `request.POST`, `request.data` offers several advantages:

*   **Broader HTTP Method Support:** While `request.POST` is limited to `POST` requests, `request.data` supports `POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH` methods.

reference: Metadata is a configurable mechanism for how the API answers OPTIONS requests (returning schema/resource info), while content negotiation is the separate process of selecting one of several representations based on client or server preferences.
reference_contexts: REST framework includes a configurable mechanism for determining how your API should respond to OPTIONS requests.
Content negotiation is the process of selecting one of multiple possible representations to return to a client, based on client or server preferences.

llm_response:
To implement custom metadata and content negotiation, you must override the respective base classes and define the logic for how your API responds to requests.

### Custom Metadata
To customize the response to `OPTIONS` requests, you should override the `BaseMetadata` class and implement the `determine_metadata` method. This method defines the resource requirements or capabilities returned to the client. Once created, you can apply your custom metadata class globally by setting `DEFAULT_METADATA_CLASS` in your configuration, or you can assign it individually to specific views.

### Custom Content Negotiation
To customize how the system selects parsers for requests and renderers for responses, you must override the `BaseContentNegotiation` class. You are required to implement two specific methods:

*   **`select_parser(request, parsers)`**: This method evaluates the incoming request and returns the appropriate parser instance from the provided list, or `None` if no suitable parser is found.
*   **`select_renderer(request, renderers, format_suffix)`**: This method determines the response format by returning a two-tuple containing the selected renderer instance and its associated media type. If no renderer is acceptable, it should raise a `NotAcceptable` exception.

Like metadata, these custom schemes can be configured globally using the `DEFAULT_CONTENT_NEGOTIATION_CLASS` setting or configured on a per-view basis.

### How the Mechanisms Decide
*   **Metadata:** The decision is handled by the logic you define within your `determine_metadata` implementation, which is triggered when a client sends an `OPTIONS` request.
*   **Content Negotiation:** The default mechanism selects a renderer based on the client's `Accept` header and the priority/ordering of the renderers configured for the view. More specific media types are prioritized over less specific ones. If multiple media types share the same specificity, the system defaults to the order defined in the `renderer_classes` list. Note that "q" values are ignored in this process. If you implement a custom scheme, the decision-making logic is entirely determined by the implementation you provide in your `select_parser` and `select_renderer` methods.

## Determining the accepted renderer¶ {#determining-the-accepted-renderer}

REST framework uses a simple style of content negotiation to determine which media type should be returned to a client, based on the available renderers, the priorities of each of those renderers, and the client's
`Accept:`
header.  The style used is partly client-driven, and partly server-driven.

More specific media types are given preference to less specific media types.
If multiple media types have the same specificity, then preference is given to based on the ordering of the renderers configured for the given view.

For example, given the following
`Accept`
header:


`application/json;indent=4,application/json,application/yaml,text/html,*/*`

There are not currently any widely adopted conventions for exactly what style of response should be returned for HTTP
`OPTIONS`
requests, so we provide an ad-hoc style that returns some useful information.

Here's an example response that demonstrates the information that is returned by default.

If the requested view was only configured with renderers for

REST framework uses renderers to determine how API responses are formatted based on content negotiation. If a client provides an underspecified or missing `Accept` header, the first renderer in the specified list is used as the default. Available renderers include `JSONRenderer` for UTF-8 JSON, `StaticHTMLRenderer` for regular HTML, and `BrowsableAPIRenderer` for an HTML-based API interface.

for more details.

## Overview of access restriction methods¶ {#overview-of-access-restriction-methods}

REST framework offers three different methods to customize access restrictions on a case-by-case basis. These apply in different scenarios and have different effects and limitations.

`queryset`
/
`get_queryset()`
: Limits the general visibility of existing objects from the database. The queryset limits which objects will be listed and which objects can be modified or deleted. The
`get_queryset()`
method can apply different querysets based on the current action.
`permission_classes`
/
`get_permissions()`
: General permission checks based on the current action, request and targeted object. Object level permissions can only be applied to retrieve, modify and deletion actions.

As with
`DjangoModelPermissions`
you can use custom model permissions by overriding
`DjangoObjectPermissions`
and setting the
`.perms_map`
property.  Refer to the source code for details.

Note
If you need object level
`view`
permissions for
`GET`
,
`HEAD`
and
`OPTIONS`
requests and are using django-guardian for your object-level permissions backend, you'll want to consider using the
`DjangoObjectPermissionsFilter`
class provided by the
djangorestframework-guardian package (https://github.com/rpkilby/django-rest-framework-guardian)
. It ensures that list endpoints only return results including objects for which the user has appropriate view permissions.

## Custom permissions¶ {#custom-permissions}

To implement a custom permission, override
`BasePermission`
and implement either, or both, of the following methods:

`.has_permission(self, request, view)`
`.has_object_permission(self, request, view, obj)`

The methods should return
`True`
if the request should be granted access, and
`False`
otherwise.

Django REST framework uses permissions, alongside authentication and throttling, to determine if a request is granted or denied access. Permission checks run at the start of a view, typically utilizing `request.user` and `request.auth`.

Policies can be set globally via `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES` or on a per-view basis using `permission_classes`. To create custom permissions, override `BasePermission` and implement `has_permission()` and/or `has_object_permission()`.

Most provided permission classes do not implement object-level checks except for `DjangoObjectPermissions`. Object-level permissions are not automatically applied to list views for performance reasons or during object creation because `get_object()` is not called; the latter requires checks in the Serializer or `perform_create()` method. Access restrictions can be further customized using `get_queryset()` to limit visibility or `get_permissions()` for action-based checks.

The provided text describes three specific serializer field classes:

*   **HiddenField**: A field that takes values from a default or callable rather than user input. It is primarily used for validation without exposing fields to the end user and does not appear in `partial=True` serializers during `PATCH` requests.
*   **ModelField**: A generic field tied to an arbitrary model field that delegates serialization and deserialization to that associated field. It is used by `ModelSerializer` for custom model field classes and is generally intended for internal use.
*   **SerializerMethodField**: A read-only field that retrieves its value by calling a method on the serializer class. By default, it looks for a method named `get_<field_name>`, which accepts the object being serialized and returns the desired data for the serialized representation.

The default representation for
`ModelSerializer`
is to use the primary keys of the related instances.

Alternative representations include serializing using hyperlinks, serializing complete nested representations, or serializing with a custom representation.

documentation.

To provide JSON-formatted error responses instead of Django's default HTML pages, you can use the generic JSON error views provided by the framework. Specifically, you can set `handler500` to `'rest_framework.exceptions.server_error'` to ensure 500 errors are returned as JSON. Regarding validation errors, the framework automatically structures these to report errors per field. When a `ValidationError` is raised—such as when calling `serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True)`—the resulting response body is a dictionary where the keys correspond to the field names and the values are lists of error messages associated with those specific fields. }

If you need to customize the style of these responses globally, you can implement a custom exception handler function and configure it via the `EXCEPTION_HANDLER` setting. This function receives the exception and context, allowing you to return a `Response` object with your desired JSON structure.

The Django REST Framework manages API exceptions through classes inheriting from `APIException`, such as `ValidationError` (400), `AuthenticationFailed` (401/403), and `Throttled` (429). Developers can create custom exceptions, like `ServiceUnavailable` (503), by defining a status code, default detail, and default code. Exceptions are inspected using `.detail`, `.get_codes()`, and `.get_full_details()`.

Views handle `APIException` subclasses, `Http404`, and `PermissionDenied` to return responses typically containing a `detail` key. Custom exception handling is configured via the `EXCEPTION_HANDLER` setting using a handler function that returns a `Response` object or `None`. For standardized 4xx and 5xx responses, the `drf-standardized-errors` package is available. Additionally, generic JSON error views like `server_error` provide 500 Server Error responses.

## Custom exception handling¶ {#custom-exception-handling}

You can implement custom exception handling by creating a handler function that converts exceptions raised in your API views into response objects.  This allows you to control the style of error responses used by your API.

The function must take a pair of arguments, the first is the exception to be handled, and the second is a dictionary containing any extra context such as the view currently being handled. The exception handler function should either return a
`Response`
object, or return
`None`
if the exception cannot be handled.  If the handler returns
`None`
then the exception will be re-raised and Django will return a standard HTTP 500 'server error' response.

For example, you might want to ensure that all error responses include the HTTP status code in the body of the response, like so:


`HTTP/1.1405MethodNotAllowedContent-Type:application/jsonContent-Length:62{"status_code":405,"detail":"Method 'DELETE' not allowed."}`

llm_response:
In custom authentication, the behavior depends on whether you choose to return `None` or raise an `AuthenticationFailed` exception:

*   **If authentication is not attempted:** You should return `None`. This signals that the authentication scheme does not apply to the current request, allowing the system to continue checking any other authentication schemes defined in the list.
*   **If authentication is attempted but fails:** You should raise an `AuthenticationFailed` exception. This causes the system to return an error response immediately. It stops the process, meaning no further authentication schemes will be checked, and permission checks will not be performed.

Django REST framework determines authentication using a list of classes, setting `request.user` and `request.auth` based on the first successful class. If none succeed, `request.user` becomes an `AnonymousUser` and `request.auth` is `None`. Default schemes are configured via `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`.

Available schemes include `BasicAuthentication` and `RemoteUserAuthentication`, both of which provide a Django `User` instance and set `request.auth` to `None`. 

To create custom authentication, subclass `BaseAuthentication` and override `.authenticate()`, which should return a `(user, auth)` tuple or `None`. If authentication is attempted but fails, an `AuthenticationFailed` exception should be raised. Additionally, overriding `.authenticate_header()` allows for custom `WWW-Authenticate` headers in `HTTP 401 Unauthorized` responses; otherwise, denied unauthenticated requests return `HTTP 403 Forbidden`.

This is necessary to prevent the original exception from being suppressed by the outer property access. Python will not recognize that the
`AttributeError`
originates from your custom authenticator and will instead assume that the request object does not have a
`.user`
or
`.auth`
property. These errors should be fixed or otherwise handled by your authenticator.

## How authentication is determined¶ {#how-authentication-is-determined}

The authentication schemes are always defined as a list of classes.  REST framework will attempt to authenticate with each class in the list, and will set
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
using the return value of the first class that successfully authenticates.

If no class authenticates,
`request.user`
will be set to an instance of
`django.contrib.auth.models.AnonymousUser`
, and
`request.auth`
will be set to
`None`
.

The value of
`request.user`
and
`request.auth`
for unauthenticated requests can be modified using the
`UNAUTHENTICATED_USER`
and
`UNAUTHENTICATED_TOKEN`
settings.

## Setting the authentication scheme¶ {#setting-the-authentication-scheme}

The default authentication schemes may be set globally, using the

## Unauthorized and Forbidden responses¶ {#unauthorized-and-forbidden-responses}

When an unauthenticated request is denied permission there are two different error codes that may be appropriate.

HTTP 401 Unauthorized (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.2)
HTTP 403 Permission Denied (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.4)

HTTP 401 responses must always include a
`WWW-Authenticate`
header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.  HTTP 403 responses do not include the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header.

The kind of response that will be used depends on the authentication scheme.  Although multiple authentication schemes may be in use, only one scheme may be used to determine the type of response.
The first authentication class set on the view is used when determining the type of response
.

Note that when a request may successfully authenticate, but still be denied permission to perform the request, in which case a
`403 Permission Denied`
response will always be used, regardless of the authentication scheme.

For more details see the
authentication documentation (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/authentication/)
.

`TokenAuthentication` uses an `Authorization` header (e.g., `Token <token>`); subclassing it allows for different keywords like `Bearer`. Successful token authentication provides a Django `User` instance in `request.user` and a `Token` instance in `request.auth`. Unauthenticated requests result in an `HTTP 401 Unauthorized` response.

`RemoteUserAuthentication` delegates authentication to the web server via the `REMOTE_USER` environment variable, requiring `RemoteUserBackend` in `AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS`. It provides a `User` instance in `request.user` and sets `request.auth` to `None`. Additionally, CSRF tokens are only required for authenticated requests, except for login views.

*   **`page_size_query_param`**: Set this to a string value (e.g., `'page_size'`) to define the name of the query parameter that allows clients to specify the page size.
*   **`max_page_size`**: Set this to a numeric value to define the hard ceiling for the requested page size. This attribute is only valid when `page_size_query_param` is also set.

### How to apply the class

**Per-view:**
Assign your custom pagination class to the `pagination_class` attribute on your view:

```python
class MyView(generics.ListAPIView):
    pagination_class = MyCustomPaginationClass
```

**Globally:**
Update your `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings in your configuration file to use your custom class:

```python
REST_FRAMEWORK = {
    'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS': 'path.to.your.MyCustomPaginationClass'
}
```

Pagination can be configured globally using the `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS` and `PAGE_SIZE` settings in `REST_FRAMEWORK`, or on a per-view basis using the `pagination_class` attribute. Built-in options include `LimitOffsetPagination` and `PageNumberPagination`, the latter of which uses a `page` query parameter by default.

To modify pagination behavior—such as changing the query parameter name via `page_query_param` or adjusting `max_page_size`—you must subclass the pagination class and override the desired attributes. These custom classes can then be applied globally or to specific views. 

Pagination responses typically include the total count, links to the next and previous pages, and the results. Additionally, using pagination classes automatically displays HTML pagination controls in the browsable API.

For example, to use the built-in limit/offset pagination, you would do something like this:


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS':'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination','PAGE_SIZE':100}`

`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS`
and
`PAGE_SIZE`

`pagination_class`
attribute. Typically you'll want to use the same pagination style throughout your API, although you might want to vary individual aspects of the pagination, such as default or maximum page size, on a per-view basis.

## A note on concurrency¶ {#a-note-on-concurrency}

The built-in throttle implementations are open to
race conditions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_condition#Data_race)
, so under high concurrency they may allow a few extra requests through.

If your project relies on guaranteeing the number of requests during concurrent requests, you will need to implement your own throttle class. See
issue #5181 (https://github.com/encode/django-rest-framework/issues/5181)
for more details.

Throttling uses the user ID to generate a unique key, falling back to the request's IP address for unauthenticated requests. The allowed request rate is determined by the `rate` property on the class (via `UserRateThrottle` overrides) or the `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES['user']` setting.

To implement multiple `UserRateThrottles` simultaneously, override `UserRateThrottle` and assign a unique "scope" to each class, such as 'burst' or 'sustained'. Additionally, custom throttling logic can be created by inheriting from `throttling.BaseThrottle` and defining the `allow_request` method.

Throttling in REST framework is defined as a list of classes checked before a view's main body executes; if any check fails, an `exceptions.Throttled` exception is raised. 

Policies can be set globally using `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`, or on a per-view/viewset basis using `APIView`. Rates in `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES` are specified using a `/` separator followed by a time period (second, minute, hour, or day), where only the first character (`s`, `m`, `h`, `d`) is required for identification.

`UserRateThrottle` provides simple global per-user restrictions. For more specific control, `ScopedRateThrottle` restricts access to specific API parts if the view includes a `.throttle_scope` property. In this case, the throttle key is a concatenation of the request "scope" and the user ID or IP address, with the rate determined by the corresponding key in `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`.

The rates used in
`DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`
can be specified over a period of second, minute, hour or day. The period must be specified after the
`/`
separator using
`s`
,
`m`
,
`h`
or
`d`
, respectively. For increased clarity, extended units such as
`second`
,
`minute`
,
`hour`
,
`day`
or even abbreviations like
`sec`
,
`min`
,
`hr`
are allowed, as only the first character is relevant to identify the rate.

You can also set the throttling policy on a per-view or per-viewset basis,
using the
`APIView`
class-based views.


`fromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.throttlingimportUserRateThrottlefromrest_framework.viewsimportAPIViewclassExampleView(APIView):throttle_classes=[UserRateThrottle]defget(self,request,format=None):content={'status':'request was permitted'}returnResponse(content)`

`@api_view`

`UserRateThrottle`
is suitable if you want simple global rate restrictions per-user.

`.throttle_scope`
property.  The unique throttle key will then be formed by concatenating the "scope" of the request with the unique user id or IP address.

The allowed request rate is determined by the

reference: The router derives the basename from the viewset's queryset attribute; a ModelViewSet with only get_queryset() has none, so you must pass basename at router registration. Rule: no queryset attribute means you must set basename when registering.
reference_contexts: all () Note however that upon removal of the queryset property from your ViewSet , any associated router will be unable to derive the basename of your Model automatically, and so you will have to specify the basename kwarg as part of your router registration .

llm_response:
When a viewset lacks a `queryset` attribute, the router cannot automatically determine the base name for the URL patterns. The `basename` argument is used to specify the initial part of the view name pattern (such as 'user' or 'account'), and the router typically derives this automatically from the `queryset` attribute if it is present.

Because you have defined a custom `get_queryset` method instead of setting the `queryset` attribute, the router is unable to perform this automatic determination. Consequently, you are required to explicitly provide the `basename` argument when registering the viewset to resolve the error.

The provided text explains different types of ViewSet classes. `GenericViewSet` requires overriding the class to either mix in required mixin classes or define action implementations explicitly. 

`ModelViewSet` inherits from `GenericAPIView` and provides a full set of actions: `.list()`, `.retrieve()`, `.create()`, `.update()`, `.partial_update()`, and `.destroy()`. `ReadOnlyModelViewSet` similarly inherits from `GenericAPIView` but only provides the read-only actions `.list()` and `.retrieve()`. Both typically require `queryset` and `serializer_class` attributes, though `get_queryset()` can be used for dynamic determination. If the `queryset` property is removed, the `basename` kwarg must be specified during router registration.

Additionally, custom ViewSet base classes can be created by inheriting from `GenericViewSet` and mixing in specific actions, such as combining `CreateModelMixin`, `ListModelMixin`, and `RetrieveModelMixin` to provide only create, list, and retrieve operations.

A `ViewSet` allows repeated logic to be combined into a single class, such as specifying a `queryset` once for multiple views. Method handlers are bound to actions via the `.as_view()` method, though it is warned not to use this with `@action` methods as it bypasses router setup and may ignore settings like `permission_classes`.

Typically, viewsets are registered with a router class (e.g., `DefaultRouter`) to automatically generate the urlconf. When registering, trailing slashes should not be included in the prefix. While regular views offer more explicit control, `ViewSets` enable faster development and consistent URL configurations for large APIs. For common behaviors, base classes like `ModelViewSet` can be used instead of writing custom viewsets. Default routers provide standard routes for create, retrieve, update, and destroy actions.

There are two main advantages of using a
`ViewSet`

`View`

Repeated logic can be combined into a single class.  In the above example, we only need to specify the

once, and it'll be used across multiple views.
By using routers, we no longer need to deal with wiring up the URL conf ourselves.

Both of these come with a trade-off.  Using regular views and URL confs is more explicit and gives you more control.  ViewSets are helpful if you want to get up and running quickly, or when you have a large API and you want to enforce a consistent URL configuration throughout.

llm_response:
The issue occurs because nested writable fields are not supported by default in serializers. When you use a nested serializer like `ProfileSerializer` within `UserSerializer`, the default implementation does not automatically handle the creation of the related `Profile` object.

To resolve this, you must explicitly define a `create()` method in your `UserSerializer` to handle the saving of both the user and the associated profile.

You can implement it as follows:

```python
class UserSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    profile = ProfileSerializer()

    class Meta:
        model = User
        fields = ['username', 'email', 'profile']

    def create(self, validated_data):
        # Extract the nested profile data
        profile_data = validated_data.pop('profile')
        
        # Create the user instance
        user = User.objects.create(**validated_data)
        
        # Create the related profile instance
        Profile.objects.create(user=user, **profile_data)
        
        return user
```

By overriding the `create()` method, you manually extract the nested data from `validated_data` and perform the necessary database operations to ensure the `Profile` record is created alongside the `User`.

REST framework uses permission classes to grant or deny API access. Permissions are defined as a list and checked before the view's main body runs; failure triggers an `exceptions.PermissionDenied` or `exceptions.NotAuthenticated` exception, resulting in either a 403 Forbidden or 401 Unauthorized response.

Key permission classes include:

* `IsAuthenticated`: Only registered users.
* `IsAdminUser`: Only users where `user.is_staff` is True.
* `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`: Full access for authenticated users; read-only access (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`) for unauthenticated users.

Additionally, object-level permissions determine if a user can act on a specific model instance and are triggered during `.get_object()` calls. Permissions can be composed using logical operators: `&` (and), `|` (or), and `~` (not), with brackets for grouping.

## Object level permissions¶ {#object-level-permissions}

REST framework permissions also support object-level permissioning.  Object level permissions are used to determine if a user should be allowed to act on a particular object, which will typically be a model instance.

Object level permissions are run by REST framework's generic views when
`.get_object()`
is called.
As with view level permissions, an
`exceptions.PermissionDenied`
exception will be raised if the user is not allowed to act on the given object.

The text explains how to implement authentication and permissions in a Django REST Framework API. To manage access, `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly` is used to grant read-write access to authenticated users and read-only access to others. For the browsable API, login and logout views are added by including `rest_framework.urls` in the project's `urls.py`.

To restrict editing and deleting snippets to only their creators, a custom `IsOwnerOrReadOnly` permission class is created in `permissions.py` and added to the `SnippetDetail` view. 

Regarding authentication, the API defaults to `SessionAuthentication` and `BasicAuthentication`. While browser interactions use session-based login, programmatic requests must explicitly provide credentials (such as username and password) to avoid authentication errors when attempting to create or modify snippets.

Permissions are used to grant or deny access for different classes of users to different parts of the API.

The simplest style of permission would be to allow access to any authenticated user, and deny access to any unauthenticated user. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticated`
class in REST framework.

A slightly less strict style of permission would be to allow full access to authenticated users, but allow read-only access to unauthenticated users. This corresponds to the
`IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`
class in REST framework.

## How permissions are determined¶ {#how-permissions-are-determined}

Permissions in REST framework are always defined as a list of permission classes.

Before running the main body of the view each permission in the list is checked.
If any permission check fails, an
`exceptions.PermissionDenied`
or
`exceptions.NotAuthenticated`
exception will be raised, and the main body of the view will not run.

When the permission checks fail, either a "403 Forbidden" or a "401 Unauthorized" response will be returned, according to the following rules:

The request was successfully authenticated, but permission was denied.

Django REST framework manages API access through authentication, throttling, and permission classes. Permissions are set globally via `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES` or per-view using `permission_classes`. Global permissions check all requests, while object-level permissions apply to specific instances during `.get_object()` calls. Custom permissions inherit from `BasePermission`, implementing `has_permission()` and `has_object_permission()`, and can be composed using bitwise operators.

Key built-in classes include `AllowAny`, `IsAuthenticated`, `IsAdminUser`, and `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`. Specialized classes like `DjangoModelPermissions` and `DjangoObjectPermissions` tie into Django's model and object permission frameworks. llm_response:
For performance reasons, generic views do not automatically apply object-level permissions to each instance in a queryset when returning a list of objects. Because the `get_object()` method is not called during a list request, the `has_object_permission()` method is not triggered for individual items in the list. Consequently, permission checks for list actions are applied to the entire object type rather than to individual instances.

To ensure that users only have visibility into instances they are permitted to view, you must filter the queryset separately. You can achieve this by overriding the `get_queryset()` method in your view to restrict the results based on the current user. For example:

```python
def get_queryset(self):
    return Purchase.objects.filter(owner=self.request.user)
```

By filtering the queryset, you limit the general visibility of objects from the database, ensuring that the list endpoint only returns the instances that the user is authorized to access.

REST framework uses permission classes to grant or deny API access. Permissions are defined as a list and checked before the view's main body runs; failure triggers an `exceptions.PermissionDenied` or `exceptions.NotAuthenticated` exception, resulting in either a 403 Forbidden or 401 Unauthorized response.

Key permission classes include:
* `AllowAny`: Unrestricted access.
* `IsAuthenticated`: Only registered users.
* `IsAdminUser`: Only users where `user.is_staff` is True.
* `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`: Full access for authenticated users; read-only access (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`) for unauthenticated users.

Additionally, object-level permissions determine if a user can act on a specific model instance and are triggered during `.get_object()` calls. Permissions can be composed using logical operators: `&` (and), `|` (or), and `~` (not), with brackets for grouping.

To ensure your serializer generates fully qualified URLs instead of relative ones, you must pass the current request to the serializer's context when instantiating it. 

In your `AccountList` view, you are currently initializing the serializer without this context. You should update your view to include the request, like this:

```python
data = AccountSerializer(accounts, many=True, context={'request': request}).data
```

The reason your colleague's `ListAPIView` works automatically is that generic views, such as `ListAPIView`, automatically provide the request context to the serializer during the instantiation process. By manually instantiating the serializer in your `APIView`, you are responsible for providing that context yourself. Providing this context will resolve both the issue of receiving relative URLs and the assertion errors that occur when the serializer lacks the necessary request information to build the links.

### How hyperlinked views are determined¶ {#how-hyperlinked-views-are-determined}

There needs to be a way of determining which views should be used for hyperlinking to model instances.

By default hyperlinks are expected to correspond to a view name that matches the style
`'{model_name}-detail'`
, and looks up the instance by a
`pk`
keyword argument.

You can override a URL field view name and lookup field by using either, or both of, the
`view_name`
and
`lookup_field`
options in the
`extra_kwargs`
setting, like so:


`classAccountSerializer(serializers.HyperlinkedModelSerializer):classMeta:model=Accountfields=['url','account_name','users','created']extra_kwargs={'url':{'view_name':'accounts','lookup_field':'account_name'},'users':{'lookup_field':'username'}}`

`classAccountSerializer(serializers.HyperlinkedModelSerializer):classMeta:model=Accountfields=['url','id','account_name','users','created']`


### Absolute and relative URLs¶ {#absolute-and-relative-urls}

When instantiating a
`HyperlinkedModelSerializer`
you must include the current
`request`
in the serializer context, for example:


`serializer=AccountSerializer(queryset,context={'request':request})`


Doing so will ensure that the hyperlinks can include an appropriate hostname,
so that the resulting representation uses fully qualified URLs, such as:


`http://api.example.com/accounts/1/`


Rather than relative URLs, such as:


`/accounts/1/`

Alternatively you can set the fields on the serializer explicitly. For example:


`classAccountSerializer(serializers.HyperlinkedModelSerializer):url=serializers.HyperlinkedIdentityField(view_name='accounts',lookup_field='slug')users=serializers.HyperlinkedRelatedField(view_name='user-detail',lookup_field='username',many=True,read_only=True)classMeta:model=Accountfields=['url','account_name','users','created']`


Tip
: Properly matching together hyperlinked representations and your URL conf can sometimes be a bit fiddly. Printing the
`repr`
of a
`HyperlinkedModelSerializer`
instance is a particularly useful way to inspect exactly which view names and lookup fields the relationships are expected to map too.

### Changing the URL field name¶ {#changing-the-url-field-name}

The name of the URL field defaults to 'url'.  You can override this globally, by using the
`URL_FIELD_NAME`
setting.

## ListSerializer¶ {#listserializer}

The
`ListSerializer`
class provides the behavior for serializing and validating multiple objects at once.

#### Deserializing multiple objects¶ {#deserializing-multiple-objects}

The default behavior for deserializing multiple objects is to support multiple object creation, but not support multiple object updates. For more information on how to support or customize either of these cases, see the
ListSerializer (https://www.django-rest-framework.org/api-guide/serializers/#listserializer)
documentation below.

### Including extra context¶ {#including-extra-context}

There are some cases where you need to provide extra context to the serializer in addition to the object being serialized.  One common case is if you're using a serializer that includes hyperlinked relations, which requires the serializer to have access to the current request so that it can properly generate fully qualified URLs.

You can provide arbitrary additional context by passing a
`context`
argument when instantiating the serializer.  For example:

`fromrest_framework.decoratorsimportapi_viewfromrest_framework.responseimportResponsefromrest_framework.reverseimportreverse@api_view(["GET"])defapi_root(request,format=None):returnResponse({"users":reverse("user-list",request=request,format=format),"snippets":reverse("snippet-list",request=request,format=format),})`


Two things should be noticed here. First, we're using REST framework's
`reverse`
function in order to return fully-qualified URLs; second, URL patterns are identified by convenience names that we will declare later on in our
`snippets/urls.py`
.

## Creating an endpoint for the highlighted snippets¶ {#creating-an-endpoint-for-the-highlighted-snippets}

The other obvious thing that's still missing from our pastebin API is the code highlighting endpoints.

Unlike all our other API endpoints, we don't want to use JSON, but instead just present an HTML representation.  There are two styles of HTML renderer provided by REST framework, one for dealing with HTML rendered using templates, the other for dealing with pre-rendered HTML.  The second renderer is the one we'd like to use for this endpoint.

This tutorial explains how to improve API cohesion and discoverability by replacing primary keys with hyperlinking for relationships using Django REST framework. Key implementations include:

*   **API Root:** Creating a single entry point using a function-based view and the `reverse` function to return fully-qualified URLs.
*   **Code Highlighting:** Implementing a `SnippetHighlight` view using `StaticHTMLRenderer` to provide HTML representations of code.
*   **Hyperlinked Serializers:** Switching from `ModelSerializer` to `HyperlinkedModelSerializer`, which replaces the default `id` field with a `url` field and uses `HyperlinkedRelatedField` for relationships.
*   **Configuration:** Ensuring URL patterns are named (e.g., `'user-list'`, `'snippet-detail'`) so the serializers can generate correct links. 

When manually instantiating these serializers, `context={'request': request}` must be passed to build absolute URLs. The final result is a browsable API where users can navigate via links.

Unauthenticated requests denied permission return either an HTTP 401 Unauthorized (which must include a `WWW-Authenticate` header) or an HTTP 403 Forbidden, depending on the authentication scheme. Key technical details include:

- **SessionAuthentication:** Requires CSRF tokens for unsafe HTTP methods (PUT, PATCH, POST, DELETE).
- **Exceptions:** `NotAuthenticated` typically results in a 401 or 403 status, `PermissionDenied` results in a 403, and `NotFound` results in a 404.

### Live tests¶ {#live-tests}

With careful usage the
`RequestsClient`
provides the ability to write tests
that exercise your API views in a more end-to-end fashion than
`APIClient`
,
while still running entirely in-process against your local Django application.

Note that
`RequestsClient`
mounts a WSGI adapter and does not perform real
network I/O. It cannot be used to send HTTP requests to remote services such
as staging or production servers. For live tests against a deployed service,
you should instead use a plain
`requests.Session`
(or similar HTTP client)
configured with the appropriate base URL and authentication.
Using this style to create basic tests of a few core pieces of functionality is
a powerful way to validate your live service. Doing so may require some careful
attention to setup and teardown to ensure that the tests run in a way that they
do not directly affect customer data.

Django REST framework provides customizable pagination to split large datasets into pages, which is automatic for generic views and viewsets but manual for `APIView` classes. Configuration occurs globally via `DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS` and `PAGE_SIZE` or per-view using the `pagination_class` attribute.

Key styles include:
* **PageNumberPagination**: The default style using a `page` query parameter.
* **LimitOffsetPagination**: Uses "limit" and "offset" parameters.
* **CursorPagination**: Ideal for very large datasets, providing consistent performance and forward/reverse navigation. It requires a unique, indexed, non-nullable, non-float ordering field.

Developers can create custom pagination by inheriting from `BasePagination` or subclassing existing classes to override attributes like `page_size` or query parameters. Third-party packages like `DRF-extensions`, `drf-proxy-pagination`, and `link-header-pagination` offer further extensions. Responses typically include the total count, results, and navigation links.

Because we're using viewsets instead of views, we can automatically generate the URL conf for our API, by simply registering the viewsets with a router class.

Again, if we need more control over the API URLs we can simply drop down to using regular class-based views, and writing the URL conf explicitly.

Finally, we're including default login and logout views for use with the browsable API.  That's optional, but useful if your API requires authentication and you want to use the browsable API.

## Pagination¶ {#pagination}

Pagination allows you to control how many objects per page are returned. To enable it add the following lines to
`tutorial/settings.py`


`REST_FRAMEWORK={"DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS":"rest_framework.pagination.PageNumberPagination","PAGE_SIZE":10,}`


## Settings¶ {#settings}

Add
`'rest_framework'`
to
`INSTALLED_APPS`
. The settings module will be in
`tutorial/settings.py`


`INSTALLED_APPS=[...'rest_framework',]`

The
`pagination_serializer_class`
view attribute and
`DEFAULT_PAGINATION_SERIALIZER_CLASS`
settings key
are no longer valid
. The pagination API does not use serializers to determine the output format, and you'll need to instead override the
`get_paginated_response`
method on a pagination class in order to specify how the output format is controlled.

#### New pagination schemes.¶ {#new-pagination-schemes}

Until now, there has only been a single built-in pagination style in REST framework. We now have page, limit/offset and cursor based schemes included by default.

The cursor based pagination scheme is particularly smart, and is a better approach for clients iterating through large or frequently changing result sets. The scheme supports paging against non-unique indexes, by using both cursor and limit/offset information. It also allows for both forward and reverse cursor pagination. Much credit goes to David Cramer for
this blog post (https://cra.mr/2011/03/08/building-cursors-for-the-disqus-api)
on the subject.

To handle raw file uploads from native clients, you should use the `FileUploadParser`. Because this parser matches any content type, it should be the only parser configured on your API view.

To implement this, update your view to include `parser_classes` and ensure it is configured as follows:

```python
from rest_framework.parsers import FileUploadParser
from rest_framework.views import APIView
from rest_framework.response import Response

class UploadView(APIView):
    parser_classes = [FileUploadParser]

    def put(self, request, filename, format=None):
        file_obj = request.data['file']
        # ... handle the file_obj ...
        return Response(status=204)
```

### Key details for your implementation:

*   **Parser Configuration:** By setting `parser_classes = [FileUploadParser]`, the view will correctly handle the raw data stream sent by your mobile team's `PUT` requests.
*   **Filename Handling:** Since your URL pattern includes a `filename` keyword argument (`path('upload/<str:filename>/', ...)`), the parser will automatically use that value as the filename for the uploaded file. You do not need to rely on form fields or `Content-Disposition` headers for the name.
*   **Request Data:** Once configured, `request.data['file']` will contain the uploaded file object.
*   **415 Errors:** The `415 Unsupported Media Type` error occurs because the default parsers are likely rejecting the raw binary stream. Using `FileUploadParser` specifically addresses this by accepting raw file upload content regardless of the specific content type. 

Note that `FileUploadParser` is designed specifically for native clients uploading raw data. If you were building a web-based upload, you would use `MultiPartParser` instead, but for your specific use case of streaming large files via `PUT`, `FileUploadParser` is the correct choice.

Django REST framework provides built-in and custom Parser classes to handle various media types, allowing complex data to be processed more flexibly than standard form-encoded data. When `request.data` is accessed, the framework determines the appropriate parser by examining the request's `Content-Type` header.

The `request.data` attribute returns the parsed content of the request body, including both file and non-file inputs. Unlike standard Django attributes, it supports HTTP methods beyond `POST`, such as `PUT` and `PATCH`. For direct access to the content type, the `.content_type` property is preferred over `request.META`. Additionally, `request.stream` provides a stream of the request body. Because the `Request` class extends Django's `HttpRequest` via composition, all standard attributes and methods, such as `request.META` and `request.session`, remain available.

The provided text outlines several API parsers:

*   **JSONParser**: Parses `application/json` content into a dictionary in `request.data`.
*   **FormParser**: Parses `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` HTML form content into a `QueryDict`.
*   **MultiPartParser**: Parses `multipart/form-data` for file uploads, populating `request.data` and `request.FILES`. `FormParser` and `MultiPartParser` are typically used together for full HTML form support.
*   **FileUploadParser**: Parses raw file uploads (`*/*`) into a dictionary with a `'file'` key. It is intended for native clients; web-based uploads should use `MultiPartParser`. It uses the `filename` URL keyword argument or the `Content-Disposition` header for the filename and respects Django's `FILE_UPLOAD_HANDLERS`.

To create a custom parser, override `BaseParser`, define the `.media_type` property, and implement the `.parse()` method.
