To enable searching, you must define the `search_fields` attribute in your view. 

While you have correctly added `filters.SearchFilter` to the `filter_backends`, the search functionality requires the `search_fields` attribute to be set to a list of fields that the filter should query against.     serializer_class = UserSerializer

# Filtering¶ {#filtering}

The root QuerySet provided by the Manager describes all objects in the database table.  Usually, though, you'll need to select only a subset of the complete set of objects.
—
Django documentation (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/db/queries/#retrieving-specific-objects-with-filters)

The default behavior of REST framework's generic list views is to return the entire queryset for a model manager.  Often you will want your API to restrict the items that are returned by the queryset.

The simplest way to filter the queryset of any view that subclasses
`GenericAPIView`
is to override the
`.get_queryset()`
method.

Overriding this method allows you to customize the queryset returned by the view in a number of different ways.

## Filtering against the current user¶ {#filtering-against-the-current-user}

You might want to filter the queryset to ensure that only results relevant to the currently authenticated user making the request are returned.

`ordering`
attribute may be either a string or a list/tuple of strings.

## Custom generic filtering¶ {#custom-generic-filtering}

You can also provide your own generic filtering backend, or write an installable app for other developers to use.

To do so override
`BaseFilterBackend`
, and override the
`.filter_queryset(self, request, queryset, view)`
method.  The method should return a new, filtered queryset.

As well as allowing clients to perform searches and filtering, generic filter backends can be useful for restricting which objects should be visible to any given request or user.

### Example¶ {#example}

For example, you might need to restrict users to only being able to see objects they created.


`classIsOwnerFilterBackend(filters.BaseFilterBackend):"""
Filter that only allows users to see their own objects.

### OrderingFilter¶ {#orderingfilter}

The
`OrderingFilter`
class supports simple query parameter controlled ordering of results.

By default, the query parameter is named
`'ordering'`
, but this may be overridden with the
`ORDERING_PARAM`
setting in the
`REST_FRAMEWORK`
configuration.

For example, to order users by username:


`http://example.com/api/users?ordering=username`


The client may also specify reverse orderings by prefixing the field name with '-', like so:


`http://example.com/api/users?ordering=-username`


Multiple orderings may also be specified:


`http://example.com/api/users?ordering=account,username`

REST framework provides several ways to filter querysets. You can override `.get_queryset()` to filter based on the currently authenticated user (`request.user`), specific URL components (using `self.kwargs`), or query parameters (`self.request.query_params`).

Additionally, the framework supports generic filtering backends for complex searches, which can be configured globally via the `DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS` setting or on a per-view/viewset basis using `GenericAPIView`. The `django-filter` library offers the `DjangoFilterBackend` class for highly customizable field filtering.

`http://example.com/api/users?search=russell`

`search_fields=['username','email','profile__profession']`

llm_response:
The behavior you are observing is determined by the authentication scheme's implementation of the `.authenticate_header()` method.

When an unauthenticated request is denied access, the system determines the response type based on the first authentication class defined in the view. If the authentication scheme has not overridden the `.authenticate_header()` method, it will default to returning an `HTTP 403 Forbidden` response. To trigger an `HTTP 401 Unauthorized` response—which includes the `WWW-Authenticate` header necessary for your client to recognize it needs to re-authenticate—the authentication scheme must implement `.authenticate_header(self, request)` to return a string representing the authentication challenge.

In your `ReportView`, the `authentication_classes` are set to `[SessionAuthentication, BasicAuthentication]`. The system uses the first class in this list to determine the response type. If you are seeing a 403, it is because the first authentication class in your list is not configured to return a `WWW-Authenticate` header.

To resolve this, ensure that the authentication scheme being used first in your list is one that implements the `.authenticate_header()` method. If you are using custom authentication classes, you must override that method to return the appropriate header string. If you are using built-in classes, verify the order of your `authentication_classes` list, as the first class is the one that dictates whether the response is a 401 or a 403.

## Unauthorized and Forbidden responses¶ {#unauthorized-and-forbidden-responses}

When an unauthenticated request is denied permission there are two different error codes that may be appropriate.

HTTP 401 Unauthorized (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.2)
HTTP 403 Permission Denied (https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec10.html#sec10.4.4)

HTTP 401 responses must always include a
`WWW-Authenticate`
header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.  HTTP 403 responses do not include the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header.

The kind of response that will be used depends on the authentication scheme.  Although multiple authentication schemes may be in use, only one scheme may be used to determine the type of response.
The first authentication class set on the view is used when determining the type of response
.

Note that when a request may successfully authenticate, but still be denied permission to perform the request, in which case a
`403 Permission Denied`
response will always be used, regardless of the authentication scheme.

The issue occurs because when an `ordering_fields` attribute is not explicitly defined on the view, the filter class defaults to allowing ordering on any readable field present on the serializer. However, if the filter is not restricted, it can potentially expose fields that were not intended for public access.

To prevent this and secure your endpoint, you must explicitly define the `ordering_fields` attribute on your view. By setting this attribute to a list of specific, safe fields, you restrict the ordering functionality to only those fields you have explicitly whitelisted.

For example, you can update your view as follows:

```python
class UserListView(generics.ListAPIView):
    queryset = User.objects.all()
    serializer_class = UserSerializer
    filter_backends = [filters.OrderingFilter]
    ordering_fields = ['id', 'username']
```

By providing this list, any attempt to order by a field not included in the list—such as a password hash—will be rejected, effectively closing the vulnerability.

## A note on concurrency¶ {#a-note-on-concurrency}

The built-in throttle implementations are open to
race conditions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_condition#Data_race)
, so under high concurrency they may allow a few extra requests through.

If your project relies on guaranteeing the number of requests during concurrent requests, you will need to implement your own throttle class. See
issue #5181 (https://github.com/encode/django-rest-framework/issues/5181)
for more details.

Django REST framework throttling controls client request rates to prevent service over-use and implement business tiers, rather than as a security measure against DoS attacks. It is defined as a list of classes checked before a view executes; failure triggers an `exceptions.Throttled` exception.

Policies are configured globally via `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES`, or per-view using `APIView` or the `@throttle_classes` decorator. Key built-in throttles include `AnonRateThrottle` (IP-based) and `UserRateThrottle` (user ID or IP-based). `ScopedRateThrottle` allows specific API parts to share limits via a `.throttle_scope` property.

Throttling utilizes Django's cache framework and identifies clients using `REMOTE_ADDR` or the `X-Forwarded-For` header. Custom throttling logic can be implemented by inheriting from `BaseThrottle` and defining the `allow_request` method, with an optional `wait` method to provide a `Retry-After` response header.

`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.ScopedRateThrottle',],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'contacts':'1000/day','uploads':'20/day'}}`


User requests to either
`ContactListView`
or
`ContactDetailView`
would be restricted to a total of 1000 requests per-day.  User requests to
`UploadView`
would be restricted to 20 requests per day.

## Custom throttles¶ {#custom-throttles}

To create a custom throttle, override
`BaseThrottle`
and implement
`.allow_request(self, request, view)`
.  The method should return
`True`
if the request should be allowed, and
`False`
otherwise.

Optionally you may also override the
`.wait()`
method.  If implemented,
`.wait()`
should return a recommended number of seconds to wait before attempting the next request, or
`None`
.  The
`.wait()`
method will only be called if
`.allow_request()`
has previously returned
`False`
.

If the
`.wait()`
method is implemented and the request is throttled, then a
`Retry-After`
header will be included in the response.

### Example¶ {#example}

The following is an example of a rate throttle, that will randomly throttle 1 in every 10 requests.

`classContactListView(APIView):throttle_scope='contacts'...classContactDetailView(APIView):throttle_scope='contacts'...classUploadView(APIView):throttle_scope='uploads'...`


...and the following settings.


`REST_FRAMEWORK={'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES':['rest_framework.throttling.ScopedRateThrottle',],'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES':{'contacts':'1000/day','uploads':'20/day'}}`

for more details.

The
`AnonRateThrottle`
will only ever throttle unauthenticated users.  The IP address of the incoming request is used to generate a unique key to throttle against.

The allowed request rate is determined from one of the following (in order of preference).

The

The

`AnonRateThrottle`

### UserRateThrottle¶ {#userratethrottle}

The
`UserRateThrottle`
will throttle users to a given rate of requests across the API.  The user id is used to generate a unique key to throttle against.  Unauthenticated requests will fall back to using the IP address of the incoming request to generate a unique key to throttle against.

It is intended for implementing business tiers and preventing service over-use, rather than as a security measure against DoS attacks or brute forcing. Multiple throttles can be used to handle different authentication levels, resource-intensive services, or both burst and sustained rates.

To achieve a server-set timestamp that cannot be spoofed by the client and is not required in the request body, you should use `HiddenField`.

The `HiddenField` class is specifically designed for scenarios where you need a value to be part of the `validated_data` without exposing the field to the end user or accepting user input. Unlike a standard field, it does not take a value from the request body; instead, it takes its value from a provided `default` or callable.

You can implement it in your serializer as follows:

```python
class EventSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    created = serializers.HiddenField(default=timezone.now)

    class Meta:
        model = Event
        fields = ['id', 'name', 'created']
```

By using `HiddenField`, the field will not appear in the API input, preventing the client from setting or spoofing the value. Because it provides a `default`, it will be included in the `validated_data` during creation, ensuring the server-side timestamp is captured without requiring manual intervention in `perform_create()`. 

Note that `HiddenField` does not appear in `PATCH` requests (when `partial=True` is used), which is consistent with its role as a server-managed value.

reference: When your authenticator is invoked via request.user/.auth, an AttributeError it raises is re-raised as a WrappedAttributeError so it isn't silently swallowed by the property access. It signals a real error in your authenticator (here, KeyError/AttributeError on the missing header) that you need to fix or handle.

llm_response:
The issue arises because your custom authenticator is raising an `AttributeError` (specifically when accessing `request.META['HTTP_X_USERNAME']` if the header is missing), which is then being suppressed by the outer property access in the request object.

When you access `request.user`, the framework triggers your `authenticate` method. If your code raises an `AttributeError` during this process, Python's property access mechanism can swallow the original exception and instead report that the `request` object itself lacks the `.user` property. This leads to the confusing traceback you are seeing, where the error appears to originate from the framework's request module rather than your custom authentication logic.

To fix this, you must ensure your authenticator handles potential errors correctly:

1.  **Avoid direct dictionary access:** Use `request.META.get('HTTP_X_USERNAME')` instead of `request.META['HTTP_X_USERNAME']` to prevent a `KeyError` if the header is missing.
2.  **Return `None` if authentication is not attempted:** If the required header is not present, your `authenticate` method should return `None` rather than allowing an exception to propagate. This allows the framework to move on to other authentication schemes.
3.  **Raise appropriate exceptions:** If you intend to authenticate but the provided credentials are invalid (e.g., `User.DoesNotExist`), you should catch the exception and raise `rest_framework.exceptions.AuthenticationFailed` instead.

The framework re-raises these internal `AttributeError` exceptions as `WrappedAttributeError` to prevent them from being suppressed, which is intended to help you identify that the underlying issue originates from your custom authenticator. You should review your `HeaderAuthentication` class to ensure it gracefully handles missing headers and database lookup failures.

## Django 5.1+LoginRequiredMiddleware¶ {#django-51-loginrequiredmiddleware}

If you're running Django 5.1+ and use the
LoginRequiredMiddleware (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/middleware/#django.contrib.auth.middleware.LoginRequiredMiddleware)
, please note that all views from DRF are opted-out of this middleware.  This is because the authentication in DRF is based on authentication and permissions classes, which may be determined after the middleware has been applied.  Additionally, when the request is not authenticated, the middleware redirects the user to the login page, which is not suitable for API requests, where it's preferable to return a 401 status code.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings,
`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`
and
`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`
.  They should be changed accordingly if you need to enforce that API requests are logged in.

The provided text outlines authentication and error handling in the Django REST framework (DRF). Unauthenticated requests denied permission return either an HTTP 401 Unauthorized (which must include a `WWW-Authenticate` header) or an HTTP 403 Forbidden, depending on the authentication scheme. However, a 403 response is always used if a successfully authenticated request is denied permission.

Key technical details include:
- **Middleware:** DRF views are opted-out of Django 5.1+ `LoginRequiredMiddleware`; instead, use `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`.
- **Deployment:** Apache mod_wsgi requires the `WSGIPassAuthorization On` directive to pass authorization headers.
- **SessionAuthentication:** Requires CSRF tokens for unsafe HTTP methods (PUT, PATCH, POST, DELETE).
- **Exceptions:** `NotAuthenticated` typically results in a 401 or 403 status, `PermissionDenied` results in a 403, and `NotFound` results in a 404.

Typically the approach you should take is:

If authentication is not attempted, return
`None`
.  Any other authentication schemes also in use will still be checked.
If authentication is attempted but fails, raise an
`AuthenticationFailed`
exception.  An error response will be returned immediately, regardless of any permissions checks, and without checking any other authentication schemes.

You
may
also override the
`.authenticate_header(self, request)`
method.  If implemented, it should return a string that will be used as the value of the
`WWW-Authenticate`
header in a
`HTTP 401 Unauthorized`
response.

If the
`.authenticate_header()`
method is not overridden, the authentication scheme will return
`HTTP 403 Forbidden`
responses when an unauthenticated request is denied access.

Note
When your custom authenticator is invoked by the request object's
`.user`
or
`.auth`
properties, you may see an
`AttributeError`
re-raised as a
`WrappedAttributeError`
. This is necessary to prevent the original exception from being suppressed by the outer property access.

#### Avoiding N+1 Queries¶ {#avoiding-n1-queries}

When listing objects (e.g. using
`ListAPIView`
or
`ModelViewSet`
), serializers may trigger an N+1 query pattern if related objects are accessed individually for each item.

To prevent this, optimize the queryset in
`get_queryset()`
or by setting the
`queryset`
class attribute using
select_related() (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/models/querysets/#select-related)
and
prefetch_related() (https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/models/querysets/#prefetch-related)
, depending on the type of relationship.

For ForeignKey and OneToOneField
:

Use
`select_related()`
to fetch related objects in the same query:


`defget_queryset(self):returnOrder.objects.select_related("customer","billing_address")`


For reverse and many-to-many relationships
:

Use
`prefetch_related()`
to efficiently load collections of related objects:


`defget_queryset(self):returnBook.objects.prefetch_related("categories","reviews__user")`


Combining both
:

`classBookingsListView(generics.ListAPIView):queryset=Booking.objects.all()serializer_class=BookingSerializerfilter_backends=[filters.OrderingFilter]ordering_fields='__all__'`


#### Specifying a default ordering¶ {#specifying-a-default-ordering}

If an
`ordering`
attribute is set on the view, this will be used as the default ordering.

Typically you'd instead control this by setting
`order_by`
on the initial queryset, but using the
`ordering`
parameter on the view allows you to specify the ordering in a way that it can then be passed automatically as context to a rendered template.  This makes it possible to automatically render column headers differently if they are being used to order the results.


`classUserListView(generics.ListAPIView):queryset=User.objects.all()serializer_class=UserSerializerfilter_backends=[filters.OrderingFilter]ordering_fields=['username','email']ordering=['username']`

`classUserListView(generics.ListAPIView):queryset=User.objects.all()serializer_class=UserSerializerfilter_backends=[filters.OrderingFilter]ordering_fields=['username','email']ordering=['username']`


The
`ordering`
attribute may be either a string or a list/tuple of strings.

## Custom generic filtering¶ {#custom-generic-filtering}

You can also provide your own generic filtering backend, or write an installable app for other developers to use.

To do so override
`BaseFilterBackend`
, and override the
`.filter_queryset(self, request, queryset, view)`
method.  The method should return a new, filtered queryset.

As well as allowing clients to perform searches and filtering, generic filter backends can be useful for restricting which objects should be visible to any given request or user.

### Example¶ {#example}

For example, you might need to restrict users to only being able to see objects they created.


`classIsOwnerFilterBackend(filters.BaseFilterBackend):"""
Filter that only allows users to see their own objects.

This is not a bug in the framework; it is expected behavior. All views from the Django REST framework are explicitly opted-out of the `LoginRequiredMiddleware` because authentication and permission logic in the API is handled by specific classes that may be determined after the middleware has already executed. Furthermore, the middleware's default behavior of redirecting unauthenticated users to a login page is unsuitable for API requests, which should instead return a 401 status code.

To enforce a blanket requirement that all API requests must be logged in, you should not rely on the middleware. Instead, you should configure the global settings for your project to ensure all API views require authentication. You can achieve this by updating the following settings in your configuration:

*   **`DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES`**: Ensure these are set to require valid credentials for your API.
*   **`DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`**: Set these to enforce that requests must be authenticated (for example, by using `IsAuthenticated`).

By defining these globally, you ensure that all DRF views consistently apply your authentication and permission requirements, providing the blanket guarantee you need for your API routes.

The provided text outlines authentication and error handling in the Django REST framework (DRF). Unauthenticated requests denied permission return either an HTTP 401 Unauthorized (which must include a `WWW-Authenticate` header) or an HTTP 403 Forbidden, depending on the authentication scheme. However, a 403 response is always used if a successfully authenticated request is denied permission.

Key technical details include:
- **Middleware:** DRF views are opted-out of Django 5.1+ `LoginRequiredMiddleware`; instead, use `DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES` and `DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES`.
- **Deployment:** Apache mod_wsgi requires the `WSGIPassAuthorization On` directive to pass authorization headers.
- **SessionAuthentication:** Requires CSRF tokens for unsafe HTTP methods (PUT, PATCH, POST, DELETE).
- **Exceptions:** `NotAuthenticated` typically results in a 401 or 403 status, `PermissionDenied` results in a 403, and `NotFound` results in a 404.

This means that only authenticated requests require CSRF tokens, and anonymous requests may be sent without CSRF tokens. This behavior is not suitable for login views, which should always have CSRF validation applied.

The discrepancy occurs because `APIRequestFactory` bypasses the middleware stack where Django’s standard CSRF validation typically occurs. When using REST framework, CSRF validation is performed inside the view itself. Because `APIRequestFactory` disables this validation by default, your view is likely failing due to a CSRF check that is being triggered or enforced differently than it would be in a standard Django `Client` environment.

To resolve this and ensure your tests behave as expected, you should enable CSRF validation explicitly when instantiating the factory:

```python
factory = APIRequestFactory(enforce_csrf_checks=True)
```

Additionally, keep in mind that `APIRequestFactory` returns a standard Django `HttpRequest` object rather than a REST framework `Request` object. If your view logic relies on the REST framework `Request` object (which handles parsing and authentication), you must manually transform the request after creating it:

```python
class DummyView(APIView):
    pass

factory = APIRequestFactory(enforce_csrf_checks=True)
request = factory.post('/notes/', {'title': 'x'}, format='json')
drf_request = DummyView().initialize_request(request)
response = NoteCreate.as_view()(drf_request)
```

Finally, ensure that you are explicitly rendering the response using `response.render()` if you need to access the `response.content` for assertions, as this is not handled automatically when testing views directly with the factory.

REST framework provides three primary tools for testing:

*   **`APIRequestFactory`**: Used for testing views directly. Unlike Django's standard `RequestFactory`, it requires the `enforce_csrf_checks` option because REST framework performs CSRF validation inside the view.
*   **`APIClient`**: Extends Django's `Client` class with the same request interface. REST framework includes a few helper classes that extend Django's existing test framework, and improve support for making API requests.

The
`APIRequestFactory`

`RequestFactory`
class.  This means that the standard
`.get()`
,
`.post()`
,

,

,

,

methods are all available.

Django REST framework provides three primary testing tools: `APIRequestFactory` for direct view testing, `APIClient` for request interface testing, and `RequestsClient` for end-to-end or live environment testing. Specialized test case classes include `APITestCase`, `APISimpleTestCase`, `APITransactionTestCase`, `APILiveServerTestCase`, and `URLPatternsTestCase`.

Authentication is managed via `force_authenticate()` for direct user/auth setting, `.login()` for sessions, and `.credentials()` for headers. CSRF validation is generally disabled by default but can be enabled via `enforce_csrf_checks`.

Configuration is customizable through `REST_FRAMEWORK` settings, such as `TEST_REQUEST_DEFAULT_FORMAT` and `TEST_REQUEST_RENDERER_CLASSES`. Additionally, `APIRequestFactory` supports a `format` argument for automatic rendering. When using the factory, responses must be explicitly rendered via `response.render()`, and the resulting `HttpRequest` must be manually transformed via `initialize_request` to become a REST framework `Request` object.

### Forcing authentication¶ {#forcing-authentication}

When testing views directly using a request factory, it's often convenient to be able to directly authenticate the request, rather than having to construct the correct authentication credentials.

To forcibly authenticate a request, use the
`force_authenticate()`

The provided text outlines key considerations for testing with Django REST framework. `force_authenticate` sets `request.user` directly, but `refresh_from_db()` may be necessary if the user instance is reused across tests. When using `APIRequestFactory`, the returned object is a standard Django `HttpRequest`, not a REST framework `Request` object; therefore, setting attributes like `.token` has no effect, and `.user` only works with session authentication. To use a REST framework `Request` object, it must be manually transformed via `initialize_request`.

Additionally, CSRF validation is disabled by default in `APIRequestFactory` unless the `enforce_csrf_checks` flag is set. Responses from views tested with the factory must be explicitly rendered using `response.render()` to access `response.content`. Finally, the `TEST_REQUEST_DEFAULT_FORMAT` setting can be used to define the default format for test requests, such as JSON.
